utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Would you bring in Professor Wagenaar, please? PROFESSOR WAGENAAR, recalled. Cross-Examined by MR. TIEGER, continued.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Professor Wagenaar, you understand that you are still under the oath that you took yesterday to tell the truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you. Mr. Tieger, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning Professor. Yesterday you spoke about one of your rules concerning prior descriptions of a suspect before the lineup is prepared before the viewing is made. You indicated on a couple of occasions that you were, in terms of the description, talking about such things as whether or not the person is a man or a woman, is white or black, is dark or fair, and those kinds of broad categories. As I understand it, part of the reason for this is that recognition of faces is something of a global process, is that right? The human mind does not engage in the process of apprehending and recording individual features in a mechanical way, but we register in a very sophisticated way the entire face?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is a correct statement about face recognition. It is not something I said yesterday, but I would not disagree about this statement of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am sorry. I did not mean to suggest the latter question was part of your testimony yesterday. As a result, because it is not sort of a check list formulation, verbal processes and those kinds of descriptions do not have a great deal to do with the process of recording and recognising faces, is that correct? I see you nodding and I just have to get an answer for the record?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that -- I find it difficult to guess what the relation with, say, the rule is that you mentioned, but it is a correct statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I would presume that, for example, in the case of someone who knew the accused from before the conflict, part of the reason that it is not sensible to seek out minor or peripheral details is that this is a global apprehension process?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would not, no, I would not say that. What I would say, this rule is just -- is aimed at two things. One is to just simply save yourself time and to exclude that the witness is talking about someone who simply is totally different from the accused that you have in mind and you want to show in a lineup. The other is that in order to make a proper lineup, you need to have, say, a rough description of, say, what the foils should look like. That is only a rough description. They do not have to have all the same shape of the nose or of the ears. You just want rough categories, like colour of hair, approximate size, colour of skin, something like age. A number of those broad categories is sufficient. So it is very useful to have a description in those terms from the witnesses so that would enable you to make a better lineup. You are also right that it is quite possible that the witness knows a person very well and would still not be able to describe the person, say, in more detail than in those broad categories, because actually he would not be able to, say, well, shape of nose or what colour of eyes or so this person has. So it also would not be extremely useful to ask for more detail in such a description, although if you can get it maybe that can be useful, but this, it does not describe it, say, a witness -- if a witness cannot give such detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. When we see and recognise someone we know, we do not, if I can use sort of an analogy, record in memory all the specific details of what that person looked like on that particular day or how long his hair was or what clothing he was wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We record in kind of a visual fashion that was Dr. Wagenaar and we already have the image of that person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You have mentioned on other occasions and in some of your works, I take it, that the ability to recognise and remember faces is a rather unique and special human capacity which goes back to the very beginnings of our evolution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At least that is the scientific opinion about that specific faculty of human beings. That is, you might even say, a prewired special unit in the brain that has a specific function to recognise faces and nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You also spoke yesterday of one of your rules which -- I am sorry, before I proceed to the rules. I know you spoke about the effect and significance of the four identifications that you have been addressing. You separated those from the recognition witnesses, the 42 or so recognition witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On a number of occasions you stressed the significance of the fact that there were four, that although this might seem like a small number, indeed, it was extremely significant, and the reason is that assuming the reliability of the lineup, you do not need more people than that to show that the person selected was at the scene of the crime, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The background of that is that if the only other explanation why they pointed all at the same person is that they guessed, that explanation can already be ruled out when you have four on the basis of the very low probability.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. In fact, I think you were speaking about four because that was the number in this case. As a matter of fact, you have stated on other occasions that two identifications, given appropriate conditions with the lineup, are sufficient to establish that the person selected was at the scene of the crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, and there are two reasons for that. I stated that in the context of Dutch law and, according to Dutch law, just on the basis of, say, legal requirements, two should be enough, but I could also establish that, say, on the basis of probabilities two witnesses, say, in ideal recognition procedures satisfies, say, the sort of statistical requirements that you would want to impose. So there, I would say, statistics and law legislation go very parallel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yesterday you spoke about the period of time that you felt a witness should or should not be given when viewing a lineup. You mentioned that, in your view, a witness should be given a very specific and limited period of time within which to view the lineup and make a selection. The principle underlying that view, I take it, is that recognition is a relatively fast thing, that it does not require a couple of hours or a couple of days generally, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the issue then with this period of time is how long it takes; if it takes too long a period of time, then you become concerned that something other than recognition is going on. It is also true, is it not, that if you insist on a particular length of time that it is going to increase the likelihood that the individual viewing will attempt to conform his selection to that length of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you say that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. If you say to somebody, "Look, you have this amount of time to view the lineup and make a selection", there is a likelihood that the person, that the witness, will make an effort to conform to that period of time, to make a selection within that given period of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, usually witnesses are very co-operative. You give them instructions. They try to follow these instructions -- if that is what you mean, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure, on the other hand, if you gave someone an unlimited period of time they might take as much time as they felt they needed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is true, the question is, as they need for doing what?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Is it as much time as they need for, say, a proper recognition, or is it as much time as they need for a rather complicated process of reasoning or deduction where they try to deduce who is the target instead of, say, simply recognising him? But you are quite right; if you give them an unlimited amount of time they can start using that time for, well, we do not know exactly what. That is exactly why you do not want to give them unlimited amounts of time, because you want to control that they are involving themselves in a recognition process and not in the process of logical deduction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But giving someone an unlimited amount of time gives you an opportunity to see how much time that person may really have needed to make a selection? On the other hand, insisting that someone conformed to a particular amount of time may compel that person to make his selection faster than he otherwise would have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle, you are quite right that if you would measure the time, that would give you an extra piece of information if you record it properly. The thing is, however, that in the way identification procedures are defined, there is no rule for how we would use, say, that extra piece of information. For instance, when it runs -- to give the worst example -- counter, say, to verbal expression, how we are going to use that. The witness points at one, but then the witness spends an extremely long time at another picture, what does that mean? It leads to all sorts of uncertainties of interpretation. We have had many examples where it was argued, "Well, the witness said this, but she spent so much time looking at this picture, she must also have recognised that person". That introduces all kinds of uncertainties that, say, a proper test should not have. Therefore, in my opinion, it is better to have strict rules to predefine exactly what is a positive identification and what is not, and that sort of excludes also the difficult discussions later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In any event, that particular instruction is not particularly relevant if the viewing and recognition is all done quickly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, if the whole process is rather quick, like I read in one of the witnesses said, "Well, the whole going through the book is finished in a few minutes", that is a rather quick process. That does not -- it would not run counter to, say, my rules or recommendations, so I would not see any difficulty, a special difficulty, there. The question remains, of course, of how the pacing exactly was, because even within a process of several minutes you can show one picture a bit longer than the others. But, say, if the whole process took in the order of minutes, I would say that there is no question of excessive time and eliciting reasoning processes. What I would rather like to prevent is the process of hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I want to speak with you also about the view that you expressed about selecting or about the instruction to a witness to select just one photo in a body lineup, just one person. As you discussed yesterday, that obviates the problem that might arise if someone selected more than one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At the same time, if a witness went through the lineup and thought he recognised more than one person, in the face of that instruction, that witness would then select just one person, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you say that again?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not exactly certain what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That instruction tells a witness that he should just select one photograph, although it may be the case that the witness believes he recognises two photographs or even three photographs in the lineup?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In principle, that would hardly be possible if the witness is instructed to see whether a certain person known to the witness by name or not by name, but a certain person that the witness has seen, has met, at the scene of the crime, to see whether that person is in the lineup, it is still possible that the subject -- that the witness would say, "Well, there are two pictures of the same person in the lineup; he appears twice", but that rarely happens because the pictures are clearly representing different people. In that case, the witness can only identify no one or one, but not logically two. The problem occurs only if you instruct the witness whether he or she can recognise anybody, because then it is quite likely or quite possible that the subject says, "Well, I recognise this person. This is the man I discussed, say, about the crime, but I recognise several others as well". So that instruction to recognise, whether you can recognise anybody, is sort of inviting this problem and is, therefore, not recommended. You exclude that problem if you say in this particular case, "Well, we have talked about Mr. Tadic. Let us look. Is the Mr. Tadic that you have seen, is he among the persons that I am going to show you?" Then logically, I would say, the witness can either indicate no one or one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But the problem that you are attempting to eliminate with that instruction is one which does not work to the credit of the witness in selecting the accused's photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can you expand on that? I think my language facility .....

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If the witness selects the accused's photograph and also selects some of the foils ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: --- as being people he recognises, you have additional information which might assist you in gauging the weight to be given the selection of the accused's photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You might, but you do not know what information you have, because if you allow a witness to point at several people and the witness is, in fact, guessing, then you increase the guessing level and you do not know what the weight of the test is any more. That is why you should not do that. Sure, if the witness is truly recognising various people, you get information about whom they recognised. But if the witness is guessing, the likelihood of, say, guessing correctly, guessing correctly who the accused is, is increased, and that is exactly what the test is for, to eliminate those people who really do not have a clear image of the perpetrator and are guessing. That is why you have the foils, to exclude guessing. So if you do not assume a person is guessing, well, it is not worth doing the test anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But allowing person to select more photographs elicits the information that the person is guessing and provides additional information?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, no, it is not even that and definitely not in your case where it is logically possible that they recognise some of the others, because the others are people from the former Republic of Yugoslavia, and we have no way of knowing whether they know these people or not. No, you really are asking for troubles. You increase the guessing level too and unknown -- with an unknown amount; whereas the set up of the test is such that you kept the guessing level very low at 1/13 which is extremely good. So I would say if you have such an extensive test with 12 foils, and you took all the care to make certain that these are not people known to the witnesses, you sort of spoil your own test by after that allowing the subject to point at more people. What if they point at all 13, they say, "I know them all"? Would you say, "Ah, the witness identified Mr. Tadic"?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is right, then you have additional information with which to gauge the reliability of the witness's selection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I would say you have no additional information. You have lost a witness, because you do not know what the identification means any more.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, that is exactly right. It does not prejudice the accused; it works to his advantage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we are here stumbling over a thing that might be different between your culture and my culture. I am not used to think in whose advantage it is. I am used to think in terms of how close can we get to the truth. So I would not run tests that make it extremely easy for an accused to get off, to get off. I would try to organise tests that help us to find out whether the accused is the same as the perpetrator or not. To that purpose, I would say, you need to ask the witnesses to indicate one person or no one, but never two, three or four.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, if I may just interrupt one moment, in terms of searching for the truth, but if the witness who is looking at the foils admits that he knows all of the individuals and, even though he knows them all, he is able to select the alleged perpetrator, is that not of assistance in determining the truth, that is, the ability of the witness to identify the perpetrator, and does that not take into account the possibility that he may, having known someone, place that person in his memory as being at the scene?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you are quite right, your Honour, if you would ask a witness, "Well, even if you know them all, who of these people is the Mr. Tadic you are talking about?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ask specifically, "Even if you know them all, we are not so much interested, now we want to know of you whom of these 13 is Mr. Tadic". In fact, then, of course, you are asking the same question that I proposed and that I proposed you asked in the beginning: "You have talked about Mr. Tadic. Is one of these people the Mr. Tadic you were talking about?" After that you can also ask (and it does not invalid, say, the earlier identification), "And do you happen to know some of the others?" There is no problem there. But if you just allow them to point at an unlimited number of people and say, "Well, he might be someone I saw and he might be someone I saw", and you do not identify whom of these people is the Mr. Tadic he saw, then you are lost.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In any event, doctor, if the witness looks at the lineup and says, "That person is Mr. Tadic" or "That person is the one who beat me on this occasion" ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: --- then the problem is -----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "But, by the way, I also know some of the others", no problem there, as long as there is only one chance given to identify whom of these people Mr. Tadic is. If they say, "This is Mr. Tadic, but he also looks a bit like Mr. Tadic, maybe it is him", then you are lost. Then you have two shots instead of one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You discussed the question of reporting negative results or misses, and whether or not those might have some diagnostic significance. I believe you indicated, for example, that a negative result could be interesting or not. For example, if you know that the person viewing a lineup was 300 or 400 metres away from the incident, the fact that there is a negative result is uninteresting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Then, I suppose, that would be true for a variety of similar circumstances if the person was not paying attention or was not ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was very dark or something was blocking the view or the person was turned around to the other way so they only saw the back of them; all sorts of reasons, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Even for reasons unrelated to circumstances but more related to human memory, I presume that a certain number of misses are also expected?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, definitely, recognition is not always perfect. Even some people who have closely watched a scene might made a mistake, but if they make such statements like, "I will never forget that face, I see that every night in my dreams" or so, and then they cannot recognise, I think in that case you should interpret the negative outcome as meaning that the accused is the wrong person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is a matter of assessing all the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You point out ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I only wanted to say that negative results can be very valid and diagnostic information.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In terms of numbers, for example, you indicated yesterday that it could be significant if a lineup was shown to 50 people only four identified the accused. You are nodding so the answer to that is "yes"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, that would also depend on the circumstances surrounding the viewing of the incident by the other 46?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, so what you would need to know about the 46, is there good explanation why they failed or is there no good explanation and should you know assume that this is just representing the guessing level? That is why you have to look closely at them. You do not have just to know the number, you have to look at the conditions as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But, in any event, those kinds of numbers would cause you some concern?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If they were as large as that, yes, I think that would cause me great concern.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What if a lineup was shown to 10 people and seven or eight selected the accused?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think it would be very wise for me to make assessments of, say, various amounts and say, "Well, this is all right, this is marginal, this is whatever", because it all depends on the circumstances. The only thing I wanted to stress is you have to know about these others. Even if there is only one other, I think the Court ought to know about it because it can be very diagnostic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You spoke yesterday about a lineup which was prepared by German law enforcement authorities, the one that you viewed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I saw it for the first time yesterday, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: OK. I know you were asked a number of questions about the possible effects of seeing such a lineup. None of the four people that you were talking about, that is, the four identification witnesses in this case were shown that lineup, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is good -- well, I do not know about that, but if you say that, I would say that is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Fine. You are not aware of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, I am not aware of it. I have no knowledge about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think you know very well what they were shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: OK.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So if you say so that they did not see that, I would say that is good.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So it is irrelevant to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The existence of that lineup if they have not seen it, they have not -- there is no possible way they could have seen it, I would say it does not bear on that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: If someone who knew Mr. Tadic from before the war was shown that lineup and selected him from that, there is nothing wrong with that either, as far as you are concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If they really knew him well before the war, there is nothing that you are going to show them that would, sort of, interfere with, say, their intimate knowledge that they are having anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You would be completely comfortable with the German authorities showing such a witness, someone who knew him from before the war, a single photograph of Mr. Tadic to say, "Is that the ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- well, the reason is, of course, because their recognition, by definition, does not have, say, on logical grounds the power to place Mr. Tadic at the scene of the crime because they are going to recognise him anyway, whether they saw him at the scene of the crime or not. So, since the power of that testimony or, you might probably go, the probative value of that testimony is much more limited, you do not have to provide very difficult, intricate tests. It does not mean anything to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So the German lineup would be irrelevant for diagnostic purposes to that group as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To that group of the people who knew him really well, I would say it is irrelevant. Now, I am not -- maybe I should qualify that a little bit. I have read in the various testimonies that some of them, some of these witnesses, know him very, very well. They went to the same school. They knew him from his birth. They were his teachers and so on. They knew him on a daily basis. Some of them knew him a little bit less intimate, knew who he was, had seen him in the village a number of times or he was pointed out to them. There is a range of acquaintance there. Of course, that range may include some people who really did not remember his face quite well. For those few, the presenting of photographs may have had the effect of, sort of, refreshing their memory, so it would have mattered. But I have no clear opinion about that, because I find it not easy to make an assessment on the basis of the various testimonies what the exact range is. I know that many of the subjects knew him extremely well. They knew him on a day-to-day basis. I would say, to them, it does not matter what kind of photograph you show. But there might be a few on the other end of the range where you may have some doubts, whether, say, showing of pictures later on may have, sort of, refreshed or altered their memory, but I do not think that many of them. But I must warn you, of course, that my little table that just classifies witnesses in groups is a little bit artificial. There is a range, say, within the cells of that table.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yesterday you mentioned that there was no linear relationship between the number of witnesses who identify and the extent of probative value. Were you referring when you said that only to the issue of identification and selection from a lineup rather than recognition witnesses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think that the statement is meant for the true identification witnesses because, logically, for the recognition witnesses there would be no relationship at all because the probative value of their recognition for placing someone at the scene of the crime is low anyway. But since the others, the four, in our case, are so important, there I think it is useful to warn that 40 is not extremely better, much better, than just four, because if you assume that those four, although they identified, could have made a mistake, then the basis of that mistake, for instance, the very close resemblance between the accused and another true perpetrator, for instance, like twin brothers, if you are afraid that would have caused the mistake, you can be almost certain that you are going to prolong the mistake and repeat the mistake with other subjects, and that is "more subjects than" does not help. If you are afraid about, say, the guessing level, then four is already enough. It does not help to get to even lower probabilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I believe I understood that. I just wanted to clarify that you were talking about identifications and not talking about the recognition witnesses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is, of course, if I may add a remark, if you have witnesses who have witnessed different crimes or describing different scenes, they were not all, say, like all 52, witness to the same crime, then it could be important to have a few witnesses for each separate crime, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, that is a matter of common sense?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But that is a matter of sheer logic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right. We talked about the Doob & Kirshenbaum test yesterday at some length. That is a test which is performed by people in your field and which you performed to determine whether or not the photospread is suggestive or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That test was administered in this case to 39 subjects?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, actually I guess that would be 40 since you also made an effort to identify the ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, but that is not in the report -- only the 39 count.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: OK, but you also tried to pick out the photograph of the person you thought might be the accused when you did not know who he was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I always try -- I am always the first subject in my own experiments, but I do not count that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: OK. You picked out one of the foils?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: After you completed or perhaps during the process of performing the Doob & Kirschenbaum test you began to wonder whether or not former residents of Yugoslavia could distinguish Serbs from Muslims from Croats and so on, and wondered whether or not Mr. Tadic was the only Serb and so that you performed an experiment in Belgrade ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: --- and found that the subjects there, who were more or less representative of the witness population here, found it impossible to classify the pictures according to ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That indicated that the hypothetical problem that had concerned you did not seem to exist and had not occurred?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with the one small proviso that I made yesterday, provided that, say, the faces that they saw indeed belonged to the category of people living in the former Republic of Yugoslavia. But I must say I was quite reassured after seeing those results that nothing had gone grossly wrong in the selection of the foils, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What question did you pose to the subjects in that Belgrade experiment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question was, "We are going to show you a number of pictures. Here are a number of categories that you could insert them in, like Croat, Macedonian, Montenegrin and so on. Will you try to make a judgment or, if you cannot make a judgment, to just guess to which category these people shown in the photographs belong". So is a kind of what we call a forced choice test. They have to categorise everybody, even if they are totally uncertain, to make sure that if they do not think they can but, in fact, they can, but they are not aware of their abilities, that would come out if you forced them to guess. So, if you force them to guess and even then they cannot do it, you can be sure there is no, say, conscious ability to do it but also not an unconscious ability to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Is there any reason why you did not put in a photograph of someone or some photographs of people known to be from the former Yugoslavia to see whether or not the subjects could do that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, yes, there was a very clear reason. We, sort of, spent the whole summer of getting good pictures of people having lived in the former Yugoslavia, and that appeared to be extremely difficult. We also spent a lot of time in finding subjects from the former Yugoslavia which appeared to be extremely difficult. Only when, say, the date of this hearing came closer, I realised that I would not want to sit here and have to tell the Court that I had no information about this problem. So what I did is I contacted a number of colleagues in universities in the former Republic, to ask them whether they if we came over for two days could provide the subjects to us. They all responded positively. The University of Belgrade was the only one that opened before 1st October. In the other there were no students available before 1st October, so we selected Belgrade for that. But at that moment there was no time to produce new pictures, so we used the 12 pictures, the 12 foils in the test that you had used. I thought that was appropriate because the true question is about these pictures not about others. So, I thought if we know about these pictures, that they cannot easily be recognised as Serbs or non-Serbs or whatever, I would feel quite sure that the test itself had not gone wrong. What you proposed to do with these other pictures is something that I would also have liked to do, but that should not have prevented me doing the test with the real foils because that is the thing that really matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I take it that nothing that happened during the course of this experiment or any other review you did would cause you now to advise big city police departments that they should check to see whether the accused is Jewish or Italian and whether the photographs are .....

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In any event, your concern would be entirely alleviated, I take it, if you found that eight or nine of the photographs of the foils were persons from former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sure, the rule that I used myself was that there should at least be five foils that are good representatives of, say, the group to which the accused belongs. So if you have five of those, five or six, I would say there is a sufficient number of alternatives that, say, a guessing witness I could have used to guess at.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: By the way, I should probably clarify the chronology that led to this since it was discussed a bit yesterday. In your letter to the Prosecution after performing the Doob & Kirshenbaum test, you mentioned in one section something about this. What you said was, "If it is argued before the Tribunal that Dutch subjects have insufficient ability to distinguish the various ethnic groups, then such a test might be performed."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We discussed it and I told you that I could not see any basis for that being argued since everyone from former Yugoslavia said that that kind of distinction was not made and not possible to make.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, which, of course, leads us to the problem which was mentioned yesterday, that people do not always know what abilities they have. There are some things that we can do we do not even know we can do. You would be very surprised to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Except in this case we know now ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: --- but, in any event, that ended the matter for our purposes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For your purposes it did, for mine it did not. So I wanted to run that test to really see.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, you did not insist to me that I should get for you the information about who the foils were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I pointed out what the problem was to you and it is completely up to you to follow that up or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: OK. You also did not advise me when you began embarking on the test with the Yugoslav subjects on behalf of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I think the first test that you do is to do it with Dutch subjects because, for instance, there are a number of things in a test that are possibly suggestive and that would be suggestive to any subjects. For instance, to take a gross area, if one of the picture is larger, that would influence all subjects, no matter where they come from. So to detect, say, a number of those problems in the photospread that have nothing to do with ethnic groups, Dutch subjects would be quite sufficient and, of course, you would first take this first, this very easy step of testing Dutch subjects. It does not exclude this one single point of ethnicity, but it already excludes a number of other mistakes that could be present in the photospread.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand that. I was just asking you whether or not you advised me when you began performing the test with the Yugoslav subjects, and you did not, correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I reported, say, what they did and what they did not do. It made sure that all sort of other mistakes were not in the spread, but there is a question mark with respect to ethnicity. I just mentioned it to you that that might be a problem. The problem was big enough -- and we have discussed that -- it was big enough for me to try to go on and find out for myself because I do not like to come to Court and have to say, "Well, I do not know that. I could have done it but I did not". So I have advised you that I would try to go on and investigate this on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You were working with the Defence about that time, were you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not working with -- I am working with you trying to answer your questions. I tried to answer questions of the Defence. I am not working with the Defence in the sense that -- in the meaning that it might have in your country.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I was ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not taking sides or anything with the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: --- not asking you that question, doctor. I just wanted to know the chronology of everyone's involvement.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Or just to prevent any misunderstandings because we all come from different countries and, say, that statement might mean different things to different people.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you something about your field of study, experimental psychology. You referred, for example, to experimental data and empirical data on which you rely. I take it by that you mean experiments which are devised by people in your field to test certain theories. It is correct to say that these tests have been criticised as not reflecting real life conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, not all empirical data on which my insights are based are, say, laboratory tests. I also published the results of many case studies in which identification was at issue. I even published statistics across a number of such case studies and I am not the only one. That is quite usual in my field. There is a concern about experiments, because reality is usually always one step more complicated than, say, what we try to create in the laboratory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At least one step.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course. That does not necessarily mean that it is invalid, what you find in laboratory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We will talk about some of those case studies later. But I was ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Oh, no. I was just wondering how long you were going to go.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I am sorry, your Honour. I did not ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Might I just ask a question? I do not have the letter. Can you pass me the letter, just to see if we can -- in my country we have a saying called "cut to the chase", and I do not know that I knew what that meant for many years. It must come from movies where they are chasing someone, you know, and so they say, "Let's just get to that." If I understand the reports that you have given to both the Prosecution and the Defence, you say that with respect to the procedures that were used and the test itself, "I cannot myself make such a judgment, because too many factors remained unknown." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So you are not here today to tell the Court that the procedures that were used are wrong and that the identification or recognition was wrong, because you do not know a number of factors, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is quite correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But you have told us yesterday about the things that should be included and we went through 50 rules, well, not all of them but many of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: OK. So that is the overall report. Then if you look at what was actually done and what we received, we received first of all -- I am now referring to the Defence 91, the report you prepared, you gave, to the Defence but I understand your position -- there were 42 people who knew, who testified that they knew Mr. Tadic, and they made an identification of him. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So if I understand your testimony, though, that is acceptable and may be used unless, unless, it is used for the proposition that the accused committed the crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (The witness nods in assent)

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But you are not supposed to make that jump; it is just that they identified him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You do understand, at least I will speak for myself, that is, as a judge, someone comes and they testify and they say these things, then, of course, we have to make this judgment about credibility which one day I would like to talk to you about -- maybe you can help us; it is very hard -- but if we do not automatically assume that these 42 and accept their testimony as gospel truth, then there is not a problem, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are quite correct, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: OK. That is one of the big problems with a Judge. We will look at these 42 and we will make assessments.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We will do it in a number of ways.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is in your domain, not in my domain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Not a problem with that unless we accept it as gospel truth and do not make these credibility judgments. The problem that you did point out, though, were five persons who testified that they knew the accused and were shown the photospread. That, if I remember from our earlier discussion (because we had arguments with counsel about this), would contaminate the identification, the photo ID identification, because they knew him before. As you said very well yesterday and in a language that I had understood, that if someone knows someone before and they are given a photo and asked to identify the alleged perpetrator, it may be that they are relying upon their knowledge that they knew him before as opposed to the actual identification?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So that is a problem. It contaminates it; it should not be done.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I may add a little bit? You can do that but, logically, you do not achieve much more than or anything more than you achieved with the other 42. It proves that they know this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It does not place him logically at the scene of the crime. So, as long as again you do not jump to that conclusion, there is nothing wrong with showing the photographs. It does not help you a lot, but there is nothing wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is something you said today just a few minutes ago. I do not remember you said that yesterday. So are you suggesting that if we, as Judges, do not make this jump and assume just because five people identified him in the photospread that that, in fact, is the gospel truth and that he committed the crime, if we do not make that jump, then there is nothing wrong with the five either, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Except for that one ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Except for one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, except for the one who, as you testified yesterday, the woman who looked at the photospread and you said that if she gave a negative response, could not make the identification, and then you are not sure what happened then, but was given another chance and should not have been given another chance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So then those five, except for that one, are OK, is that correct, in terms of procedures that were followed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I suppose if that is my understanding, I do not know why we need to go through a whole lot of case studies. I do not want to cut you off, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I certainly do not mean to create problems where there are not any, but I am anticipating at least what use may or may not be made of the doctor's testimony. I want to make sure that everyone's understanding is correct. I agree that with respect to those five -- I was not concentrating on either those five or the earlier 42. I think the doctor indicated his testimony was not relevant to that group. I am merely concentrating on the four persons he said, "If you are satisfied with those procedures and you think that they were reasonably reliable, then you can be sure that the person selected was at the scene". I am focusing on the factors the doctor suggested may or may not bear on that reliability.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry. Tell me the last -- the person was reasonably at the scene. That is the problem that I have personally with the whole procedures. Just, as far as I am concerned, whether a person identifies someone and is known to them their whole life and they are in the 42, let us say, and then say not only did they know him their whole life but they saw him at the scene, well, you know, we make judgments about that; yes, it is clear that they were able -- I would accept, unless he or she is impeached, that they knew him, but that does not mean that we can say that he was at the scene unless we believe the testimony. Do you understand what I am saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course I do.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is the 42. The only reason I wanted to ask the question was that yesterday, as I recall, Mr. Wladimiroff asked the witness, well, these 42, the identification, something to the effect, that that cannot be used that they committed the crime. Dr. Wagenaar said, "Yes, that cannot be used". I just wanted to make it clear that I do not think anyone who has been in the judging business for any amount of time would make that jump, for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: As Judge Stephen pointed out, your Honour, it was clearly not why the dock identifications were made. At the time the first witness came in to make a dock identification, we had that brief discussion about it and it was clearly acknowledged that it was being used for a certain purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Right. So there the identification was only confirming that this is the person they have known for all of these years. It was not a recognition or identification just based on seeing someone sitting between two guards. I suppose where I am is that that is the 42. Now he says that the five, you know, why give them the photospread if they knew them before. That was something that was considered also, at least in my mind. That was something that you and I discussed. I mean, you know, we can disregard his looking at the photospread and just say that the man testified he knew him. I remember when the testimony came in. Why are you showing them a photosprad if they knew him? Except for that one woman who was given the opportunity twice, perhaps, it was not really clear. But all of this has been spent on the four who did not know him and who were given a photospread. In the letter that Professor Wagenaar writes you, he tells you, that is the Prosecutor, "I conclude that the spread of 13 photographs can be used for identification purposes". That is what he does. You can use them. Those are the four. Yesterday he spent a lot of time going through all of the rules saying what should be in, but he does not know whether that was not taken into consideration. So all I am suggesting (and I have talked too long myself) is that I did not know why you were going to get into the case studies. But then you say you have to respond to the direct, because you do not know what the Defence is going to do with the testimony. I suppose you do not know what the Judges feel about it either. So you do not know how far to go. Is that what you are saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is partially true. The Court will get information about the procedures that were used and will then be in a position to make the appropriate judgment which is for the Court about the weight to give the identifications. I am just trying to avoid a mechanical application of rules in a book without a reasonable understanding of where they come from, what they might mean and what impact they may or may not have on the identifications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: While the flow of cross-examination has been interrupted -- I am afraid I might have been responsible for that and I apologise to you -- there is something basic that I have failed to understand in this witness's testimony from the start. It was repeated again this morning. He obviously knows what he is talking about and I am misunderstanding, but continually I seem to hear that the probative power of the evidence of those who knew Tadic well from childhood and who then say, "I saw him at a certain place" is less than that of the four identification witnesses who had never seen him before and saw him on one occasion and then identify him. I would have thought it is exactly the opposite. I think the witness said this morning that the 48 recognition witnesses, the strength of the probative power (I think it was the expression used) of their identification is low. I would have thought it is infinitely higher than the case of the four and of great significance. Can you perhaps ask the witness to elaborate on this?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Can I just expand or comment on that too? Maybe it is because we are so interested in this area -- I am. For those four, if they did not know him before, then you can eliminate any possible bias, reason for lying, anything, because the only way that they can identify him is using the photospread and that is why that is so powerful. But as to those 42 who said they have known him and then told us about a number of things, that is when the credibility judgments come in, for me at least, that I have to apply. But for those four, it is very powerful because they did not know him before, if you accept that, and then you exclude any possible bias ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Oh, no.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- no? That is not true because ----

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: No. I mean, they may be grossly biased.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: --- they might be grossly biased and it has been alleged because of different religious -- but is that what you are saying about those four?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: What I am saying is that -- I am not talking about the probative value of, say, the total testimony of witnesses. Of course, those who knew him very well, they know what they are talking about and about whom they are talking. What I am saying is for those who knew him very well, the identification does not add a lot. That is not an important extra piece of information. Of course, they can identify him. It does not tell you a lot about, say, whether the other part of their story is a true story. Identification does not help to make that decision because they can make that decision anyway. For the four who did not know, identification helps a lot because if they are true -- if their story is not a true story, they would be totally unable to identify him and the fact that they are able to identify him needs an explanation. If you still believe their story is not true, now you have to explain for yourself, how was it possible that they identified him? It points at the truth of their story. So for those four, the identification is an important extra piece of information, whereas for the 48 it is not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: I understand ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am not talking about the total probative value of their testimony, because there I think you are quite right, those who knew him very well are probably far more important than the others.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I understand then -- thank you very much -- exactly in relation to the 48. I would like you, if you would, just to tell us a little bit more about why the probability is that the four are not lying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the four may still be lying ----

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: --- about what they saw. But if they are all able to identify him, they must have met him somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the only logical possibility is that they have met him in the camp, that places the accused in the camp.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is still possible that he did not -- there he did not do what the witnesses say, but at least now he is placed in the camp. If he denies ever having been in the camp, there is something to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If he would have said, "Ah, but I have been in the camp, of course they know me, but I did not do those things that they accuse me of", then you still do not know very much. But if he takes, say, the position, "I have never been in that camp", they recognise him, we need an explanation how that is possible because guessing is simply out of the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I think that clarifies my difficulty I had.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You can go on, Mr. Tieger. Go on with your case studies. I think you know, at least, what my understanding is and what Judge Stephen's is as well. OK. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. [To the witness]: Just to alleviate any undue concern on the part of the Court, when I refer to case studies I was talking about what will probably be a 45 second recitation of a few factors that are significant.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I am sorry. I spoke too long then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Doctor, I think we were discussing at that point a little bit of information about your field of expertise and talking about the kinds of studies involved. The fact of the matter is, as you indicated, that these experimental studies are conducted in such a manner because of pragmatic reasons that forced you to use laboratory conditions rather than real life circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Doctor, I am talking about the empirical studies themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, right, I do not agree with that. Doing statistical analyses of real cases, real trial cases, is still empirical research. Those are empirical data. Second, I am not quite sure what you mean by "laboratory studies". Some studies are very realistic studies in which we create a very realistic situation outside the lab. We test the witnesses of those situations just in exactly the same manner as you would test them. The only, say, lab-like aspect of it is that we have created the situation so we control it, we know exactly what has happened, but otherwise those situations can be very, very realistic. Maybe I may explain to you that just in the last year one of my students has completed a thesis that will be defended next year in which we compared, say, a very difficult situation in 22 banks that we have created. Of course, the managers of the banks agreed that we would do that. But the cashiers and, say, people, employees of the bank did not know at all that they were tested, they were subjects and so on. We did -- we involved also person recognition with identity tests, so many person photospreads and so on, just like you would do it with a real, say, unexpected bank robbery. We compared that with, say, exactly the same situation on television, because one of those occasions we have filmed on television, and we have showed that in the lab to subjects who knew they were subjects and were simply watching a TV episode of something that happened in the bank, and we asked them to do the photospread and so on. The result is that you find almost no difference between how the bank employees performed in the photospreads and what you would call the laboratory subjects performed. So, I have no -- point (1) is that many of the experiments are under very realistic conditions, that is one, and that can be done, it is not easy but you can do it, and point (2) is that from this study the difference with lab conditions is not necessarily high; in some of the studies it is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But the reason for moving towards more realistic conditions is that such factors as arousal, motivation, attention are believed to be different in real life situations than laboratory conditions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the reason is that you do not want any uncertainty about that, just as I did not want any uncertainty about the role of ethnicity. You want to be certain that it is not such an important factor. That is why you want to make the comparison. It is not because we believe that it is important, because then we would -- if you believe that, we would immediately come to the conclusion that we cannot do lab studies. No. The reason that we make the comparison is that we want to exclude that it is terribly important. If you can exclude it, then you can base some of your recommendations also on lab studies. I must say, although, if you go through the 50 rules that we discussed yesterday, that you will find that the large majority is based on logic, not on psychological lab studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But where based on lab studies you would agree, would you not, it has been argued that laboratory studies on identifications are invalid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It has been argued (and probably we both know, are aware, of the literature), it has been argued but not demonstrated, and the argument is that, sure, it must make a difference. But at that time that these first publications appeared, there was no empirical demonstration that showed convincingly that it makes a big difference and that, therefore, the recommendations that were based on lab studies would be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Have you yourself not acknowledged that, although there may be partial solutions to the problems raised by those critics, there is much truth in that argument?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, there is much truth to the extent that if you have not ruled it out, you have a problem and you cannot logically argue that lab studies are good enough. You have to rule it out. So there is, as long as you do not know, there is a problem. But once you have made the comparison I have just described you once that we did ourselves in my group, you can rule it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So it is possible to alleviate the problem, but the criticism of the fact that those conditions are different is valid?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would say the claim that the conditions can be different is valid. The claim that it matters is not so valid. Let me give you a very simple example. If you want to buy new eye glasses, you can go to an opthamologist and he has some sort of letter chart, and you read those letters and you see what the best eye glasses are. You do not expect the opthamologist to have a courtroom because you want to use your glasses in the courtroom. The test done by the opthamologist is good enough and makes it possible to generalise to the courtroom situation. If you can look well on the letter chart, you can also look well on the courtroom. So, the generalisation from the lab to reality is always something a scientist should consider. But it is not, by definition, an obstacle. It is something you ought to consider. If it has not been considered, the criticism is completely correct. We do not know anything about this, we have not studied it, do not without having this knowledge just assume that the validity is there and apply it, especially not in cases where, say, the weight given to it could be extremely large and the consequences very large. But once you have studied it and you see that the generalized ability is there, the problem has gone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is the point the critics were making, in that it ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, say, that Egeth and McLoskey, they are among the most -- the initiators of that criticism, I think. It has not been properly studied and it was, I think, a totally just worry that they verbalized. Right now I would be much less worried. I see you are going through a book that I know well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So, at least more recently, efforts have been made to remedy that problem and to resolve that problem? As of 1992 you were still quite concerned about that problem?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not really. It is becoming maybe a bit repetitive. The problem addresses only those recommendations that are purely based on, say, research. For instance, the recommendation that I have made based on our own research that you should have at least five foils, not three or four but five, because then the test is optimum. It is based on research in the lab and in realistic conditions. There is a set of experiments, not just one experiment, and there is a comparison of those experiments, and the general finding is in realistic conditions and in lab conditions that five would be enough. You might say, well, that is a recommendation that follows from research. It is, of course, also partly just a logical rule. The guessing level is simply computed by, say, 1 divided by the number of foils. You can just say, if we have five foils, the guessing level is 1/5th, 20 per cent. There is no lab research involved in that. You could, completely independent of research, argue, well, four foils it would be 25 per cent. Is that acceptable? You can build some sort of reasoning on the basis of simply the guessing level. I think the two reasonings coincide. The five that follow from the empirical research I think coincides with the thought that a 20 per cent guessing level and then a number of witnesses, so that you multiply those guessing levels, leads to a fair amount of certainty. If you have two witnesses, 20 per cent, times 20 per cent is -- and then you are down to four per cent. I would say, well, that should be acceptable. A total certainty does not exist in criminal law.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that is an appropriate time.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is a very good place to stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Dr. Wagenaar, your report (which was sent to Mr. Wladimiroff and a copy of which was also sent to the Prosecution) addresses the most important concerns about the reliability of a lineup or photographic parade. For the most part, that document may speak for itself but I want to ask you about at least one of the factors that you discussed in there. You referred to the possibility of biased instructions. I know that yesterday you indicated that, in your view, it is highly important to tell a witness expressly that the wanted person may not be in the lineup. You have mentioned that a couple of times.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You indicated yesterday that the research on the presence or absence of that explicit statement shows that it has a large effect on false positives?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is meaning the selection of foils instead of the accused. You also indicated that the research on that is reported in the chapter which precedes the chapter in your book on rules?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is chapter 2 and, indeed, in it you refer to biased instructions and the case study cited is Malpass and Devine?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, however, Malpass and Devine did not involve an instruction which said, for example, "If you see anyone you recognise in the lineup, point him out". Instead, it involved the following instruction, "We believe that the person who pushed over the electronic equipments during the EEG demonstration is present in the lineup. Look carefully at each of these five individuals in the lineup. Which of these is the person you saw push over the equipment?"

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is the biased instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is the biased instruction in Malpass and Devine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The unbiased instruction contains the warning.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: So that the Malpass and Devine study on which you rely is a contrast between an instruction in which one test a portion of the group is given an instruction in which they are explicitly told that the person may not be in there, contrasted with another group which is told expressly that the person is in there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I think you should also read out the unbiased instruction used by Malpass and Devine so that we can make a comparison of what is the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Sure. "The person who pushed over the electronics equipment during an EEG demonstration may be one of the five individuals in the lineup. It is possible that he is not in the lineup. Look carefully at each of the five individuals in the lineup".

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This study, however, was a contrast between the effects of those two instructions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It was not a study of an instruction which says, "If you see someone you recognise in the lineup, then point him out"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, because that instruction, in fact, is never given in lineups. It is always an explicit reference to one particular person mentioned by the witness in his or her testimony. So I do not know of any studies in which the instruction is studied say, that, well, was reported in the records like, "If you recognise anyone, please indicate who it is". So there is very little that I can say about that specific instruction. The only thing I have said about that specific instruction is that it may create logical problems, because if they recognise totally correctly more people, what do you do? So I have not said that that more vague instruction is biasing or anything. I said that it may create logical problems and I do not know whether it has created logical problems or not in this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Doctor, I indicated earlier we would talk about case studies and I indicated to the Court it would be very brief.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: 45 seconds.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It is always a mistake, your Honour, but I think we can cut to the chase on this. In fact, in, I guess, 1990 you wrote an article on examples of circumstances in which bad procedures were followed and were criticised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you referring to the article co-authored by Elizabeth Loftus?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is right. I just wanted to run down some of the examples of such bad procedures that you identified in the course of that article in your efforts to find examples of bad procedures. I am not sure how well you recall the article, so I ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not have it in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: --- will just summarise it briefly then and you tell me if that is correct. In one of the studies, the perpetrators were wearing full face masks leaving only their eyes visible. The two witnesses who ultimately identified a perpetrator said they initially could not recognise anyone because he was masked. There was a one person lineup. In another, every foil differed in at least one significant way from the accused. The lineup size was only about four?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There was repeated testing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In another, there was a one person lineup and repeated testing and the witnesses knew the accused from before. In another, the effective lineup size was three. The suspect was the only one in a distinctive item of clothing and there was a repeated testing. Another, there was a one person lineup. All the details of the prior descriptions were incorrect. In another, the photospread was made up of completely possibly suspects. There were repeated tests. Witnesses talked to each other during the course of the actual identifications. In another, there was a one person lineup. The witness knew the accused before. Police specifically mentioned the accused's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They are horrible examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In another, the lineup only had four foils. There was repeated testing and there were actual suggestions to the witnesses to change their identifications. In another, there were five foils. Two did not fit the description at all. Both witnesses knew the person from before the incident, but stated they did not recognise him at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In another, the instructions were that the suspect definitely was in the photospread and, in fact, he did not fit the description given by the witnesses previously. Thank you, doctor. That is all I have, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Professor, yesterday we discussed about the length of time that would be appropriate to show the photographs to the subjects, to the witnesses; today it was being discussed again. Let me just to clarify some points: is it true that the longer the time is given to the witness to look at the photograph, the more time the witness has or there is more risk that the witness may reason or may attempt a logical deduction of his choice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I would say, starting from a certain period, a certain presentation period is reasonable and beyond that I think you would increase that risk. I would argue that maybe up to half a minute per picture would be, say, within reasonable limits. Beyond that, I think you would be asking for trouble.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Talking about time and looking at the picture, let us move to a related matter, a live view, a live situation, where a witness will see someone. Did you research anything on, for example, the problem of a fleeting glance?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Fleeting glances.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Dr. Wagenaar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That was not covered in cross-examination and is certainly beyond the scope of this cross. We focused on entirely different matters.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: A live situation -- was that discussed in cross and is it even present in this case, a live lineup?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I am not referring to a live lineup, your Honour. It seems to me a related question to how much time you need to ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Identify.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: --- identify, what would that be in live? That is what I am trying to test here, is there any difference or what?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: The objection is it goes beyond cross?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It seems not to me, your Honour, because it has been discussed the time of looking is relevant here. So I want to explore whether there is any difference in time, whether you look at the picture or look at the person in live.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The questions were only directed to the question of how long a presentation period there is for a witness viewing a lineup. The doctor just answered that question.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I do not recall that Mr. Tieger asked any questions on cross how long it would take in a live situation to properly identify or recognise a person. That is the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I understand that and it has not been asked by Mr. Tieger. It seems to me it is a related question. It relates to the same problem, how much time do you need to identify, live or from a photograph?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: He says that was not discussed.
