utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The time ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: These photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It has been discussed how much time would be needed from a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour -- I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I will overrule the objection for the reason that are our rules are very liberal. We admit all evidence that is relevant, that has probative value, and we may exclude it if it does not. Since we only have 10 rules of evidence, we really do not have any rules that talk about extent of cross and going beyond. We, though, applied them as the trial has gone on and we apply them differently, I suppose, sometimes. But I will overrule the objection. You may get into it, even though I do not remember anything on cross that got into it. You say it is related. Go ahead, Mr. Wladimiroff.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. (To the witness): You may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think we should make a clear distinction between two situations. One is the situation in which the witness saw someone commit a crime or just saw someone, and that was the first time that the witness sees this person. So it is the first impression of a certain person. So that is not a recognition because it is the first encounter. It is the sort of imprinting the image of a person you did not know yet. Fleeting glance, technically, usually is referring to this situation, because if in that situation you see a person for a very short period, you might not receive a good enough impression of that person to be able to recognise that person later. For instance, in British law fleeting glances during the first encounter, sort of, rule out identification tests, because the first impression cannot have been good enough. I think your question refers to the second situation where now the witness is asked to recognise a person, so that is possibly the second encounter -- that is what you want to know, is this the second encounter or not -- and recognition, recognising a person whom you have encountered before can go much quicker. It can be within the second that you say, "Ah, ha, that is him". So, for a recognition, say, a very short presentation should not rule out the acceptability of the response of the witness. On the contrary, if the witness would need a very long time you would say, "Ah, ha, but that cannot be a recognition because recognitions usually go very quick". So, the presentation time for the second situation, the recognition situation, need not be very long, whereas for the first situation you may require that it is reasonably long, long enough to form a good impression of a person. Now, if your question is how much time do you need for a recognition, what is a reasonable presentation time, I think I have to repeat my answer. Anything between zero seconds and half a minute would be totally acceptable for recognition. If a witness needs more than half a minute to recognise a person, you may doubt whether that is a true recognition.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But if a witness after two second says, "That's him", I would say that is totally acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Another matter I want to clarify is the German photospread that was shown to you yesterday. Again, to be absolutely certain about this, would it be relevant if the four witnesses you mentioned yesterday and today, the four witnesses we all focused on, had been involved in a German photospread, in this German photospread?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, then, say, the photospread, the 13-person photospread that was reported in the records, would be a repeated test, and it is not certain any more why they recognise the face because they have seen this person at the scene of the crime or in a previous test. So that would be extremely relevant, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. You were also asked questions by the Prosecution about the instruction. Am I right in thinking that it all comes down to two issues, whether the instruction is open or whether the instruction is more precisely formulated? I think you mentioned that if you ask, "Do you recognise anyone?" you run the risk that people will recognise more than one person, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, or some -- simply it is even -- the risk is even bigger. What if they try to recognise, say, a limited set of people that they have in mind and do not realise that maybe someone out of that, outside that set, could be present? Then they are not even telling, maybe not even telling you that the one person you are interested in is in the set. So you really run a risk on all sides. It might be that the witness is telling you far more than you want to know and you cannot interpret it any more. It is also possible that the witness is exactly not telling you what you want to know, although the witness could easily have done that and you just miss information.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Theoretically, you might have two situations here. You start with a test with the witness and then you interview the witness or you start the interview with the witness and some way on the road or at the end of the interview you run the test. Let us focus on the first one. If the test was run freshly without a previous interview, what would be the correct instruction to tell the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it is very difficult then to give a correct instruction because the correct instruction mentions, say, one particular figure that needs to be identified. Also, it would be rather difficult because, ideally, you would first ask the witness to describe that person. In some conditions, you then have to stop because you have to construct the test on the basis of that description. So, if the first thing that you want to do in the encounter with the witness is use the photo test, then that photo test would logically not be based on any descriptions that the witness gave. So you are already in trouble. No, the logical way of doing it is interview the witness, asking the subject -- asking the witness to describe the person, say, that might be present in the test, and then ask the subject, "Well, this particular person that you described to me, is he present in this photo parade or live parade or not?"

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: What if the test was run and afterwards a description was asked?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, then you run a great risk. You first present the test. It is possible that -- let me give you an example, a very simple example. You have constructed a test. All foils really look like -- look like the accused, so it seems to be an unbiased test. But now the witness says, "Ah, but the person I saw had a little scar just under the eyes", and if you look well you can see the accused has that and the others have not. Well, once the witness has that information but you did not know because you first applied the test, it is, of course, extremely easy for the witness to identify the one person because that one person has the scar and the others have not. In that sense, given that piece of information is not a fair test any more. So you first want to know what is the information that the witness already has, and can we find foils that, sort of, show all these characteristics that were presented by the witness? Now, that might happen, so you run a great risk. It might be all right because the witness is not giving you any more details that now invalidate the test, but since you do not want to run that risk, I would say, first, you ask for a description, then you look at the test and say, "Would this test be a fair test for this witness?" Then you go on. Let me give you an example. We have had in Netherlands the rather famous case of the killings in a supermarket in Oosterbuk Albert Heijn supermarket. In that case we had to construct, because the witnesses gave different amounts of detail, different lineups for all subjects, for all witnesses. There you simply could not use the same live lineup for every witness. So, first, you have to ask their descriptions, then you construct the lineups.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. Would that mean that the records of the test should place the test in sequence with the interview? So if we only have the record of the test itself, should we also not know when the test was run during or after the interview or at what stage of the interview and when the description was given by the witness, should that be indicated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. You also testified this morning again about the Belgrade experiment. Why did you run that experiment? Was that on the request of the Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I just ran it -- I informed both Prosecution and the Defence that I was worried about this detail and that I would try to run an experiment on this, just to be sure about this detail, but we run it on our own initiative. No one requested it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You testified also that the subjects with whom you ran the test were students from the Belgrade University, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Do you know their ethnic descent?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In fact, we do, because since we were there we ran some more experiments with them and for those other experiments we had to know. We left it open for them because if they refused to indicate or they did not feel any ethnic belonging, they could also indicate that, but most of them indicated their ethnic descent, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could, if I would inspect the data, but I have not the data with me and I do not feel certain enough to -- but there was some spread of ethnic background there, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. We discussed yesterday (and it has been indicated today again) the ethnicity of the foils. What if the foils were not from the former Yugoslavia, would that be relevant for the test you ran in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think if they were -- if none of them was from the former Republic, then there is a second explanation why they could not classify them and that explanation would not be like the first, that simply there is no difference or it cannot be perceived, but it was a meaningless task because they simply do not belong in those categories. So, it would be important to know that, I would say, the majority of them, or the large majority of them, really came from the ethnic Republic, and if then they still cannot classify them, that means that, say, that faculty, that ability, does not exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The majority or a large majority out of 13 would mean six, seven, eight, something like that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I would say, eight or nine out of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If not, the Belgrade experiment may be explained in a different way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and is, in fact, quite meaningless.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Focusing on the four again, the Judges put some questions to you and following the line of questioning I have some questions on that issue too. Say just for the sake of the argument that those four have lied about their not knowing Dusko Tadic before. If that could be established or if the Judges do not believe that they told the truth about that, would that have any influence on the outcome?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I mean, that is not a proper question for almost any witness I can conceive of, but certainly not for this witness in his capacity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: It seems to me ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: I think if you rephrase the question to ask him what effect would it have on the validity of the test if they had not told the truth about not knowing him, that is a better way to put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Rather than getting into our province. So I will overrule the objection, Mr. Tieger, or do you think that is still objectionable? You are free to object to anything I say. I am sure you lawyers do when we are not around!

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: The Doctor has commented at length about the factors which he considers to be significant or not in assessing the reliability of a test. Now to go back over the same ground in the context of characterisations of a witness's testimony seems to me to be inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: You spent a lot of time on cross talking about the four, as a matter of fact most of time on direct and cross has been on the four. I will overrule your objection. Again, try not to invade the province of Judges. Try to get this witness to focus on the validity of the tests and whether they have been conducted according to acceptable, professional standards. That is really his help for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour. I do adopt the way you have phrased it. It is my bad command of the language I could not do that right away, but I may pass the question to the witness if he wants to answer that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If the four witnesses knew Mr. Tadic before the war, that places them in the other group. First of all, there is nothing wrong with the test, but the impact of the test changes now because their identification can do nothing else but confirm that they know him. It does not place him any longer logically in the camp. But there is nothing wrong with having performed those tests on those people. It is only the implication of it that changes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Is it relevant to consider that they might not be aware of knowing him before, thinking they tell the truth about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, it is possible that you honestly believe never to have met a certain person while in fact you have met him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: You mean live, in person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be a live encounter. It could be you have seen a picture of this person on television or in a newspaper or wherever. For instance, maybe it has happened to you that you are looking at, say, a film or a movie on television and it takes you half an hour to realise you have seen this movie before. You were not aware of it then and suddenly something happens and you say, ah, but I have seen this before. So it is quite possible that you have seen something, someone and you are not aware of it. The question whether that unconscious knowledge would help you to identify and you still honestly believe that you identify him for another reason, that is a very difficult question. But that again cannot be excluded. It is a risk.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Does the test eliminate that risk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the test does not logically eliminate that risk. If a person has had a previous encounter but does not know about it or at least does not tell you about it, there is no way to eliminate that possibility through a test.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. They told us they knew him before, they did not know him before, those four did not know him before, and they identified him through the test, and I leave aside whether this test was run properly or not. The mere fact that they recognised him, does that mean automatically and logically and exclusively that they have seen him at the place of the crime? Could it be the case that they might have seen him elsewhere and therefore recognise him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You have to establish that can be excluded within all reasonability, I would say, because at the end of course there is nothing you can establish for certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Does that mean that the test itself ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: But I would say the more witnesses you have who recognise him, the more unlikely that explanation will be because now you have to assume that that is the case for all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: But that means ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: So the reason for having more witnesses is to sort of exclude all those small things that cannot really be excluded on the basis of logic or evidence, but by increasing the number of witnesses, and I would say four is a reasonable number, now you would have to assume that all four have seem him and lied about it or all four have seen him and do not realise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If all talk about the same event?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they all talk about having seen him in Omarska, that is the thing you want to establish through the test.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only that, have they seen him in Omarska or not. It does not matter what they saw him do in Omarska, that might be different, but what they say is, "We saw him in Omarska" and if they did they must be able to identify him now. So it does not matter which event.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: The test itself, am I right in thinking when I say that the test itself does not exclusively place Mr. Tadic in the camp? You need more to establish that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, you need -- but those are the 50 preconditions that I have listed. Once you violate these conditions you have difficulty of interpretation. It does not necessarily invalidate the test. It becomes now more difficult to interpret for the Court what the identifications mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Say, having met him before the war is one of those preconditions. I even think it is number one that I have listed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Coming to these rules, they might have emerged from laboratory tests and have been tested in reality. Are those rules adopted anywhere in legal practice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there are variations from one country to the other. I think the United Kingdom is the most strict, after a number of identification disasters I must say, more strict in the adopted rules. I think your colleagues could explain to you in more detail what the rule in their country is. In the United States, but I think the President can tell more about it, I think the rules vary from one State to the other slightly. In the Netherlands there is a code, some sort of code adopted on the basis of what is called de Recherche Advies Commissie, investigatory, advisory committee, who have adopted a very good strict set of rules that is used as, say, a guideline to the Court of what is to be expected from investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Are the rules you have formulated in your book we have been talking about yesterday and today reflecting the same issues, the same procedures, the same ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: --- concerns to avoid ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they are. I was a member of that committee when these rules were formulated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all I ask.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, any recross?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Doctor, the issues about which your formulated rules are concerned are issues of identification and reliability and so on. So when you say that the countries you mentioned which have adopted certain guidelines or rules for the conduct of investigations reflect the same issues, does that mean that any country has adopted your 50 rules wholesale?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Various countries have in one form or another addressed themselves to the same issues in various ways?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and even before I formulated my rules, of course. Almost nothing is original in the rules I have stated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That is all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Nothing arises, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Professor, I wanted to ask you something quite different and a preliminary question. Am I right in thinking that you are expert in the question of human memory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, you are correct. That is my general field, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: I wonder if you can help me in relation both to facial hair and also to uniforms. If you have a situation in which a person, we will call him a witness, sees someone and at the time he sees him there is of course no question of his having some years later to give evidence, how likely is it that that person will three or four years later recall whether a man possessed or did not possess at the time (A) a beard and (B) a moustache? I segregate them because it seems to me, with due respect to yourself, that a moustache is less obvious than a beard? Have you any views on that as an expert?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have, your Honour. I have done research on moustaches and it depends sometimes on the moustache. Some well-known people have moustaches that are not being remembered and others have moustaches that you simply cannot miss. But the general experience is that if -- and we have run an experiment with one of my colleagues in law and psychology who has a moustache who was presenting a course for 10 weeks, two hours a week and at the end of the course we asked the students to describe professor so and so. His moustache was missed quite a few times, whereas I would say I found that always a quite remarkable moustache. So that happens. There is nothing to worry about and you definitely cannot conclude if a witness does not describe a moustache or says "I cannot remember a moustache" that the witness has never encountered this person. It is quite possible. It is also the reasoning why in my letter to Mr. Wladimiroff I said do not worry too much about the facial hair issue; it is probably a very misleading issue.

utterances.speaker: THE COURT
utterances.text: Then imagine a country in which very many people are wearing uniforms. Again, a person sees a man and some years later is asked to describe what he was wearing. How likely is it that the witness would know whether or not, remember whether or not the person was wearing civilian clothes or a uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, we have a lot of knowledge about that on the basis of records from the former German concentration camps and extermination camps, and the reports that people gave about uniforms not about, say, uniforms they have seen, but who was wearing what uniform, are not so very reliable. Again, it does not mean if the witness describes a person with a uniform he could never have had, that still does not mean that the witness has not seen this person. It only means that the witness has seen this person, also has seen this uniform and now sort of transposes the uniform from one person to another person. We know from experience, as I said, that that might easily happen and there is no doubt whatsoever that those witnesses have been in those camps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE STEPHEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: There is just one matter that arises your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Professor, do people memorise, remember colours if they remember a person?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you referring to colours of clothing?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is very well possible. If you are asking about the nature of a memory, is a memory a picture and a coloured picture, that is a far more difficult question because you can remember if you have, if the memory is in fact some sort of A verbal description, that verbal description could still, say, contain a description of colours, but if you ask can people reproduce the colours they have seen in their oral testimony,, the answer is, yes, they can.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: If we deal with uniforms, not one colour uniforms but multi-colour uniforms ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Like camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Yes. Will people remember the components of such a uniform or would they remember the image as a total one colour or a mirage of colours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The most likely thing to happen is they remember, say, a camouflage uniform because you can remember that as a word, you do not have to remember the colour. It is rather more likely if you would ask what colours, that they might refer to a camouflage uniform they have seen recently and come up with those colours instead of the colours they really have seen. So, I would be hesitant to ask such a question and I would not attach very much weight to the answer. I would say the camouflage uniform instead of a beautiful parade uniform. So I would say that is very significant, but I would not ask for specifications of what kind of camouflage uniform because there is a lot of confusion possible there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you. That is all I ask.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Professor Wagenaar being permanently excused?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We may want to recall Professor Wagenaar, your Honour. We do not want to release him on our side because if the Prosecution is going to produce additional material, as seems to be the case, then we want to recall Professor Wagenaar again. It may also be technically in rebut to the rebuttal, but that is a matter for the Court to decide.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: At some point we have to end. I was going to look at the Rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: I am just announcing that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Without in any way suggesting we can go back and forth forever, Dr. Wagenaar, you are free to leave now. However, you may be recalled as a witness to testify. So please make yourself available, but you are now excused. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff or Mr. Kay would you call your next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, might we adjourn for lunch early today and perhaps resume before half past two? The two witnesses called earlier this week in closed session will be required by the Defence to be recalled so that your Honours can hear further evidence. They are due to go back later on today. So it is important that we try to locate them. We know where they have been taken to but they are not immediately available.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yes, your Honour, I have no objection to that, but there is a matter that I would like to mention in closed session and we could use the next 10 or 15 minutes for that.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: That is a very good idea, because I have a schedule appointment and will not return until 2.15. So we could not begin earlier because we plan on recessing from 1.00 until 2.30. So we will then use this time for you, Mr. Niemann, and we will go into closed session. So we will stand in recess for five minutes to go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: (The Court adjourned for a short time).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Perhaps, your Honours, it may be appropriate for me to renew in open session an application that I made to your Honours just immediately prior to the luncheon adjournment. As your Honours are aware, in the course of these proceedings the Prosecution called a witness who was given the pseudonym "Witness L" and who gave evidence in camera relevant to certain allegations contained in the indictment but, in more particular, in relation to paragraph 4.3 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Of count 1?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Of count 1, your Honours. I have previously handed to your Honours a copy of the indictment where I have indicated the allegations that I think are relevant to the testimony of this witness, your Honours. Your Honours, over the period of the past couple of weeks following evidence that was called by the Defence in this case, the Prosecution has carried out an investigation into Witness L and into certain matters relevant to him and to his testimony. Your Honours, as a consequence of those investigations, the Prosecution now feels that it can no longer support that witness as a witness of truth. We invite the Chamber to disregard his evidence entirely. We, in so doing, acknowledge, your Honours, that in relation to the allegations brought forward by this witness in his testimony that they are no longer standing and, as a consequence of that, in relation to those matters the accused has no case to answer and we invite your Honours to rule accordingly. In addition to that, your Honours, we have had certain discussions with the Defence and it seems appropriate, your Honours, that the Prosecution call a witness who can give further details relevant to certain things that were said by this witness, in particular, in a conversation between this witness and members of his family. With your Honours' leave, I will call investigator Robert Reid from the Office of the Prosecutor who can relate to the Court the circumstances that brought the Prosecution to this position. I now do so, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, does that accurately reflect the agreement that you have reached?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is right, your Honour. I am grateful to my learned friend for dealing with this matter so promptly at this stage of the trial.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you. Would you call in Mr. Reid, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: If your Honours, please? MR. ROBERT WILLIAM REID, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Reid, would you please take the oath that has been handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Fine. Thank you. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Investigator Reid, I think you have previously testified before the Tribunal ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --- in relation to these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Your full name is Robert William Reid and you are an investigator with the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: You are also the lead investigator in relation to the case of Dusko Tadic ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: --- in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Yesterday afternoon were you approached and requested to arrange a meeting here at the Tribunal between certain parties?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Who were the parties that you were requested to arrange this meeting with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Between the witness, (redacted), a gentleman by the name of Janko Opacic and a gentleman by the name of Pero Opacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The witness (redacted), have you known him under a pseudonym, pseudonym "L", up until this stage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you then proceed to arrange this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Where was the meeting to take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: To take place in the Prosecution room on this floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: The witness (redacted), where is he being held at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What arrangements did you then put in place in relation to this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I spoke with the secretary, I think, to the Deputy Registrar for a travel order to be struck for him to be brought to the Tribunal this morning at 10 a.m. which occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you also have a conversation with a representative of the Defence in relation to their attendance at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had a conversation with the Defence this morning in relation to where the interview would take place, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you describe the circumstances of the interview, from best you can remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I have made a statement in relation to this and if I can refer to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Might I seek the leave the Court for Investigator Reid to refer to it, if necessary?

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you have a copy of it, Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I do and there is no objection. It is a contemporaneous note.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Basically, what occurred this morning was at about 10 past 10 I met with Mr. Janko Opacic and Mr. Pero Opacic in the office of the Victims and Witnesses Unit. I then went with them and an interpreter to the interview room here and at that time I was accompanied by Miss de Bertodano from the Defence and Mr. Petrovic who, I believe, is the investigator for the Defence. We walked into the room where (redacted) was seated and I said to him that I had two persons that I would like him to meet. Janko and Pero Opacic followed me straight into the room. I then asked if he know either of these two persons and he stated that he did not. I then asked Mr. Janko Opacic whether he recognised (redacted) and he said, "Yes, that is (redacted)", and then I asked Pero Opacic whether he could identify (redacted) and he said, "Yes, that (redacted)".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: So at this stage (redacted) still denied that these two gentlemen that you had with you were his father and brother, respectively?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What happened then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We then left the room, and I had a quite short conversation with Janko and Pero Opacic. I then entered the room again and I had a conversation with (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Can you relate that conversation you had?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was basically that I believed that Janko Opacic was (redacted)and I also believed that Pero Opacic was (redacted), and then outlined a number of investigations that I have carried out during the past two weeks which led me to that conclusion. I said that I was 99 per cent certain that I was correct, that they were (redacted), and that I would be 100 per cent certain on Monday or Tuesday when blood sampling comes back.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did he say to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He still denied -- he said, "(redacted). I do not know why you are bringing people before me. You are endangering me", but continued to deny that they were any part of (redacted) (redacted).

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did you then do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I then went and I spoke with Miss de Bertodano for a short time, and then I had a conversation with Janko and Pero Opacic in the presence of Miss de Bertodano. There were two things that were worrying me. One was that he would not admit it in front of me or, secondly, there was something that was in his mind that had blocked it out totally. So we decided that the best thing would be to just confront them together, sitting in the room together where they could just sit quietly, the three people, Janko Opacic, Pero Opacic and (redacted). That removed me from the room, but if it was something that was blanked out in his mind, I asked Pero Opacic if he could just talk to him and, perhaps, stimulate something in his mind, to say something that he may remember that only those two had done, perhaps a football game, perhaps a birthday party or something that may stimulate something. That was done. After some time, I think probably 20 to 25 minutes, I went back into the room with the interpreter and I said, "Has anything been resolved?" or words that effect, "Has anything been resolved?" and he said, "Yes, this is (redacted)". He said, "Yes, (redacted), Janko Opacic, and (redacted) (redacted) Pero".

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What did he say to you then after he told you this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, at that time I went and got Miss de Bertodano and Mr. Petrovic. They came back to the room with me and I confirmed that again in their presence and then we all left the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: What was the next thing to occur?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I then went back to the room with the interpreter at about 12.30 p.m. and I again had a conversation with (redacted). The first thing I asked him was why he had lied about the death of (redacted), and why he refused to acknowledge photographs that were put to him in the Court as (redacted). He apologised and he told me that he had something to tell me. He then stated he had been set up by the "Bosnians". He said that after he had been captured -- when he was captured in about November 1994 he was shot. He was captured as a member of the Serb Army and at that time he was interviewed by the military, and he had been beaten by the interrogators.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Did you understand what he meant by the "Bosnians"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the Bosnian government authorities, and at that time I believe it would be, my understanding is that it is the Bosnian government military, the army of the Bosnian -- Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Thank you. Go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He stated that he was told that he had been in the camp by the interrogators, and that he did, in fact, know Dusko Tadic, I then asked him if he, in fact, did know Tadic and he stated that the first time he had seen Tadic was on a video shown to him (redacted). I understand that to be when he was transferred from military custody into civilian police custody.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: He did not indicate to you who showed him this video?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he has indicated a certain person whose name I cannot recollect at the moment, but I do have in some records and I am attempting to find that out now.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: Go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He said that after his initial interview by the military, he was transferred (redacted) where he spoke with police interrogators for seven hours a day for about one month. The purpose of these conversations was to train Witness L -- (redacted), I am sorry, to give evidence against Dusko Tadic. The training took the form of watching videos of Mr. Tadic and watching videos of the Trnopolje camp. He said that after that training was complete, he then took part in the taking of a statement that was signed by him. I then asked him was he actually a guard at the camp and he told me that he never was. I asked him how he knew the layout of the camp and the surrounding areas so well. He stated that he used to play football with his friends, and sometimes

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: within the grounds of the camp. He also stated that he used to pass the camp on occasions and saw detainees within the camp. I then asked him why he had pleaded guilty to something that he had never done. He stated that he had been threatened that if he did not co-operate with the Bosnian authorities he would be executed, and I took this to mean that he would be murdered as opposed to an execution by a lawful court order. I then asked him about the identification of (redacted) (redacted) that he related to the Bosnian authorities, and he stated that they had told him that (redacted) (redacted) had worked with him in the camp, and once he had got that knowledge, to protect (redacted), he told them that (redacted) was dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: In relation to these matters that have just come to light, have you had an opportunity to do any further investigations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not at this stage, not as a result of what has occurred today, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No further questions of the witness, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just one matter and that is if you can help me with this matter, Mr. Reid? Do you know how it was that Witness L, (redacted), came about to become a witness in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the Tribunal was contacted, or the investigation section at the Office of the Prosecutor was contacted, I think, in March 1995 that there was a potential witness in relation to the trial of Mr. Tadic. I travelled (redacted), I think, in April 1995 and had an initial interview with him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Which body or organisation provided the contact with this witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is the investigation department of the Bosnian government, the police investigation department.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is all I ask.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, do you have additional questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: I have nothing further, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Is there any objection to Mr. Reid being permanently excused? I ask that question each time and, of course, Mr. Reid is with the Prosecutor's Office, but it has become routine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I think, as the officer in the case, he will probably be staying with it anyway, your Honour, so I am not sure anyone really wants him released.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Then you will around, will you not, Mr. Reid ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: --- until we finish the case, in case you are asked to return to give testimony by counsel or by the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: So you are now excused. Thank you very much for coming.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, would you call your next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, we call the accused Dusko Tadic. MR. DUSKO TADIC, called.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Sir, would you please take the oath that is being handed to you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good. Thank you. You may be seated. Mr. Kay, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you give the Court your full name, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dusko Tadic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: October 1st 1955 in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is your father or was your father called Ostoja Tadic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What is your mother's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My mother's name is Staka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you have brothers Mladen, Stojan and Ljubo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it right that your brother Ljubo gave evidence in these proceedings recently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, his real name is Ljubomir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Were you brought up in Kozarac and was that the place of your family home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was born in Kozarac, like my other brothers, and that is where I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us what your education was? Were you educated in the local school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I completed elementary school in Kozarac, like all my other brothers. After elementary school, I continued my education in Belgrade where I completed my secondary schooling.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Do you have any academic or other qualifications for trades?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I completed secondary school for TV mechanics in Belgrade, a technical school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you left school what was your first job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I first started working in Cajavec, the company Cajavec, in Banja Luka. That was at the beginning of 1981, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that an electrical company?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it is an electrical company, a well-known firm manufacturing TV sets. I think it is the only such factory in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: For how long did you work there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked until 1984 or '85.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was your next job, having finished work at that factory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My next job was private business. Around 1987 I opened a private company in Croatia in the town of Sisak, and I worked with that firm until 1989, in various parts of Yugoslavia, but it was registered in Sisak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have a partner in that business?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, my partner was my long-standing friend, Solkonovic Fikret, and while we were working in the territory of Croatia and Slovenia, and afterwards another friend joined us from Kozarac, but he was not an official partner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In between those last two jobs you have told us about, did you work in Libya or did you go to Libya and stay there for some time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think this was in '85 or '86. Actually, I spent up to six or seven months there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the reason for going to Libya?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The main reasons were economic problems in former Yugoslavia. Life was getting difficult. Some people were doing well, but we always wanted to do better.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you get any work in Libya?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, my wife got a job as a nurse, so I left with my daughter. I hoped to get a job but that did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You have told us about your wife. When were you married?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was married in 1979, but officially we were not married. Only after our first daughter was born we actually got married.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How many children did you have within that marriage?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My oldest daughter is called Valentina. She was born on 11th April, 1981. The younger daughter's name is Aleksandra, 4th March 1989 is her date of birth. The older one was born in Banja Luka and the younger one in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did there come a stage when you and your wife went through divorce procedures?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, upon our return from Libya we agreed to divorce and we did, me and my wife, and this lasted for quite some time. Actually, we never got officially remarried again, but this was something that never really concerned us. We did not care much about it, the actual official marriage or divorce but when we lived together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What was the reason for having that divorce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, from the first day I wanted to go abroad and upon return from Libya I did not have a job. We had no livelihood from friends from -- some friends from Switzerland promised to find a job for us and that it would be much easier if we were divorced. First of all, my wife is a nurse, a medical nurse, and for medical staff it was quite easy to find jobs abroad if they were divorced, and that is the only reason for our divorce.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So was your wife trying to find employment abroad that would have been easier for her to obtain if she did not have officially a husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that was just the -- you had to provide a document certifying that you were not married.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Throughout your marriage has that been the main occupation of your wife, working as a nurse?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she graduated secondary medical school, I think it was called Maglajic in Banja Luka, and she worked in that profession all her life.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did she work in hospitals around Kozarac? Can you tell us which hospitals she worked in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From 1980 she worked in Kozarac. At that time she had -- the place where she was working was a health centre, though it belonged administratively to the Prijedor hospital. She worked in Kozarac, then for a time after that in an outpost in the village of Kozarusa, and occasionally she would work at the outpatients clinic in Trnopolje. Then for a time she would be a visiting nurse on the territory of Kozarac. These were mostly the jobs she had until she left Kozarac in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At some stage after April 1992 did she resume her nursing work in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, she started working. I think it was August 1992. She also worked in the Prijedor health centre. It is, so to speak, the same institution only located in Prijedor because there was no such post any more in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have heard about your family. Were you a close family, a family that had good relations amongst you, sons, with your parents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly, yes. Nothing special, there is nothing special to be said about that. When we were younger, of course, we were extremely close but as we grew up, since there was a considerable difference between me and my eldest brother -- my eldest brother is nine years older than me -- we were not so close because of this large difference. As we grew up and were ready for secondary school, some went on to higher schools. Most of my brothers left Kozarac for their education. Then they went to Banja Luka, Belgrade, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have heard that your eldest brother, Stojan, travelled around the former Yugoslavia and was in business, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for a time he worked in Banja Luka in an enterprise called Veletekstil and afterwards as a travelling salesman for the same firm, and several years before the war broke out in Bosnia-Herzegovina he worked as a travelling salesman for his own firm. He had some partners but I do not know them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is it right that he was unable to continue in business as relationships between the states of the former Yugoslavia deteriorated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The second son, your brother Mladen, is it right that he went to work and live in Germany?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When was that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he left in 1973 or '74. He went to Munich and there he worked in the Siemens company. After that he worked in several private companies. All this went on until, I think, March of 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did your brother Mladen keep up close contacts with the family in Kozarac? Did he visit them frequently or infrequently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he came very frequently. From the first day he left for Germany, already after a year or a half, he would say that he would be coming back next year and this went on for 25 years. All people who went to Germany went in the belief that they would come back in two years time. He was very tied to our place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The third son and your other brother, Ljubomir, is it right that he went to live and work in Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When Mladen left for Germany -- I think this was in '73 or '74 -- he went to Banja Luka where our older brother had lived there before. He lived with him for a time. At the time -- at the same time he engaged in karate coaching. Afterwards he got a job in Cajavec and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have heard that three of the sons of the Tadic family, Ljubomir, Mladen and yourself, have all been karate experts with black belt and having the fifth, fourth and third dan as grades amongst you, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The titles in karate are right, but to call us "experts", I think that is rather a broad term and perhaps it would be suited to Mladen who lived in a large west European centre. To a part, it could apply to Ljubomir who was among the more well-known competitors and coaches, but it could not be said of me, least of all of me, because I sort of went with them, but I did not have any special merits in that field.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you coach karate within Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I was an amateur coach of a club which was founded in 1981 in Kozarac based in the Kozarac elementary school. When I had time, I would conduct the coaching, but I was linked more to the Borac karate club in Banja Luka because in Kozarac I was working mainly with children aged seven to 12 mostly. There were no older members of the club.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We heard from your brother, Ljubomir, that his club in Banja Luka was the Borac club. Was that a rather bigger scale karate club than what you were running in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The club in Kozarac was, one might say, insignificant for a long time. We were not even registered as a club because of the age group of the participants. We did not have any competitors. We mostly competed at the level of children, but the club in Banja Luka was a big one, a well-known one. It was founded by our older brother, Mladen, and when he left for Germany Ljubo continued to head the club and one could even make a living of that. This was not possible in Kozarac. This was just amateurism, recreation, nothing more.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you take part in sporting competitions yourself, in karate competitions and matches, representing either your club or a local association?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For a time I did compete for the Borac karate club. There were several, one in Banja Luka, one in Belgrade and that is all. I was not a competitor. I mainly engaged in sport for my own satisfaction, and those who wanted to join with me. That is why I took part in the opening of the club in Kozarac. Many parents wanted this. It was an inexpensive sport. It did not require great funds. So that my participation in that sport in Kozarac was mainly educational, that is, I dealt with small children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: How long did you run the karate classes at the school in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I officially led it. I was a registered coach, officially registered coach, but I had assistants from the first day. These were younger boys. I did not have so much time. From 1981 until I went to Libya I travelled to Banja Luka daily. I had to work in my company every working day and that is quite a distance from Kozarac. At first, I did not have my own car and even if I did it would be expensive to travel. I would get up at 4.35 a.m. and take a bus on the Prijedor to Banja Luka road at Kozarac at 5 a.m. We would get to Banja Luka at 6.00. I would get back at 6.00 or 7 p.m. the same day. So that I would spend two to three hours travelling, the rest working, and what time I had left I would be with my family. Occasionally, I would go to the club just to encourage them to develop the sport. I did not have time to dedicate myself to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you ceased running the club at Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When I left for Libya in the previous few years several younger people had grown to competitor status, so there were people who wanted to continue the work of the club, and as of then I mostly -- I did not really engage in leading the club in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It has been said in evidence that you were someone who would have been known in the area because you featured on the sports pages of the local newspapers such as Kozarski Vjesnik. Do you recollect being on the sports pages regularly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were often reports about my brothers, Mladen, Ljubomir. Mladen was one of the best known people in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Yugoslavia as a master karate competitor, Ljubo too. But, as far as I am concerned, I do not remember such articles. There was no reason. I never won any competitions in Yugoslavia. I competed only a couple of times, so that there was no significance in that. Active sportsmen and competitors would have competitions at least twice a month. I did not have time for any such thing, and I did not look upon karate as a competitive sport.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did your brother Mladen represent Yugoslavia at international competitions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think he did several times at the international level in Hamburg. I do not know whether he was in Paris. I think he was. He did participate in several international competitions in Belgrade every year, in Sarajevo. He had a great deal of success, so did Ljubomir as a karatist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did Ljubomir also represent Yugoslavia internationally?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for quite some time he competed together with representatives of a special karate style at various competitions in Europe and throughout Yugoslavia as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you represent your country at international level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not even at the Republican or inter-Republican level, no, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What sort of level of competition were you in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I participated in three competitions in all, as a competitor, but I participated as a coach and I took children to compete at these competitions. So I would be sitting there with the audience somewhere. My job was to take care of technical things, applications, travelling to and from the venue, giving advice such as coaches do. That was all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you continue with that work or did there come a time when your involvement in that aspect of karate ceased?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As I said, Kozarac did not have a competitive club for older members. Upon my return from Libya, I decided to go in for private business and dedicate myself to business and the family. So my sporting activities were reduced to recreational activities and contacts with friend. I had no participation in any public competitions from then.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When you got married, did you live at the family home in Marsala Tita Street that we have seen photographs of during this case?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you always live there or did there come a time when you moved to live in another house or place in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not live there all the time. Around 1987 or '88 I lived in a house in Kalate Street in Kozarac also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Having lived there, did you eventually return to live with your parents back at the Tadic family home in Marsala Tita Street?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after our father died in 1989, somewhere around August, I returned to live in the family home in Marsala Tita Street in Kozarac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would like you now to look at Exhibit 300 which is a photograph of the family home. If it could be put straightaway on the overhead projector? You can turn to the right. Thank you very much, Mr. Usher. As you know, we are very familiar in this courtroom now with this photograph and I want to run through this fairly quickly. We have been told that on the left-hand side is what is today a bar which originally was given to your brother Mladen by your father, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Next to that where the wider windows are, those are premises that are run by your brother Ljubomir, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [The witness indicated] Yes, at this time it is now a business space but it used to be a residence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The smaller window to the right of that is where your other brother Stojan was given a portion of the family home, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. All these three parts had separate entrances from the outside.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Originally, your parents' home was a single storey home where you and your other brothers were brought up, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It is this part. [The witness indicated]

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The extra floor on top of the ground floor, that was built at a later date, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. This part here was built first and later on this one here, up here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who lived in that upper storey above those ground floor sections that were eventually given to your brothers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the first period, when I first got married, I lived here. [The witness indicated]. Then I moved to Kalate and after the return I lived in this part here. [The witness indicated] Somewhere around 1990 I moved to this residential unit here. In 1990, this part was not completely finished inside and I completed it together with my wife and only then did we move in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have heard about your father. He was an eminent person in Kozarac because of his distinction in the Second World War, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He was a well-known participant of World War II in 1941 and, not only that, because he was a well-known participant, he was also an honest and realistic man. He was 90 per cent handicapped because of the wounds he received during the war. That is on the one side. On the other side, he was also known as a man who was a very tolerant man from the World War II on regarding things national, and this is precisely why he moved to Kozarac in 1946 and continued to live there until his death. Throughout his life he continued to build this house, for one reason he wanted one -- he only needed one business unit but he wanted us all to come back and live there. He did not need all this space.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As a former army officer, is it right that he was given a reasonable pension?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, those were among the largest pensions in Yugoslavia at the time. It was a pension at a level almost like an average German salary of an average employee in Germany. So it was a good pension, and the very fact he was able to put all his children through school with that money and build a house talks about that. Plus, he had other privileges, ability to raise loans and then he had free trips to the coast. He never travelled by train. He would always take planes and he was a very sick man.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The right-hand section of the family home that we see in that photograph was built at a later date, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can you tell us when that right-hand section was built?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You think this part?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: No, on the ground floor which is slightly -- no, over on the right-hand side where the Nipon cafe was.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I showed it once.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes. When was that built?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Construction of that part of the object was completed in 1990. The construction was started by -- I started about a month before my father's death in the summer of 1989. However, gathering of all the materials for this structure took much longer. From the first day when I went to Libya and when I opened the private business in Croatia, in the period between 1977 and '89 which means, 87, 89 when we lived in the Kalate Street, I was always in the field. I rarely ever got there, maybe two or three nights a month. I was always working in the field. I was with my company in Ljubljana, Zagreb, Belgrade, and my time was always on construction sites. It was a construction company. I am saying this because by working in the field I would come back to Kozarac every once in a while and gather the construction materials that I would need for construction of this structure, and so I started it in '89 and finished towards the end of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Eventually, there came a stage when you opened a cafe in that side of the house, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, towards the end of 1980 -- '90, that was in December and January.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The upper part of that side of the house in red brick, was that built at a slightly later time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was built at the same time. The basic construction work was done by the end of 1990, but I was concentrating on the lower part for economic reasons so that I could start the business as soon as possible, calculating that if I use that money I could build the rest, but both were planned as a single business premises and the top part was never moved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You completed the bottom part and then work on the upper section still remained to be finished, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in fact, I never stopped working. When I first opened my business, from the first day, I continued with the construction. I was gathering more materials. I was putting in installations. I was reckoning that until '92 or '93 I would open the other part of the premises and so that I could move my family, because the brother Ljubomir wanted to have this lower part where I was, that I was occupying at the time, turned into business space.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The finance for that section of the house which you had your cafe built upon, did you obtain loans from various local people in order to contribute to the costs of the building?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The expense, the costs for this construction were very high. In any event, a lot of people helped me. My neighbours, friends, even relatives, would show up by themselves and offer to support that. Some offered labour, some offered financial aid, some without interest, some of the people came to my mother's. They knew that I was also building my residence where we wanted to move to. There were even people who offered it for their own economic interest. In that period, all dinar means were very difficult to raise. Adem Kahrimanovic is a good example. He had a lot of means in the local currency, dinars, but he could not raise them in value, and that in those circumstances we made an arrangement that he would give me about 10,000 deutschemarks at the time and I would give it back to him, but I needed to return it to him in dinar counter value. At that time I had to do it, it would be about 15,000 deutschemarks at a time by the time I returned it, so there were different ways in which people helped me and there were some economic reasonings in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did occasions occur when a number of local people would gather together and a sheep would be roasted and sections of the house would be built with a number of hands giving support?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that was a tradition in Kozarac. I do not know about the other parts, but Kozarac had that tradition. It was not a question whether you had money to pay people. It was a tradition which lasted, I do not know how long. When there were larger construction works, if you had to put the roof or put a concrete plate on top, then all neighbours would come over. I remember when there were cases when two brothers, they were not -- they did not have a good relationship, they did not even have a contact, even though they were relatives, but the family members would always go there, regardless. It was an old tradition in those parts. The host -- it was an unwritten rule -- would either put a pig on a spit and they would give out the drinks, and it was not material benefit, it was a tradition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What time did your cafe start to trade and you receive customers from within Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In December 1990 I started -- I started trading in this cafe Nipon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In that period until the conflict in May 1992, was it a successful business?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I thought that it was successful. I thought it was a success. I never worked as a waiter there at any time. I was the owner of the cafe and I mostly did other jobs which was supplying and then dealing with the tax authorities and local administration, pay rolls and such, but I thought that it was rather successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was it a place that was particularly popular with the youngsters in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, mostly the young people. I think that the average age of my patrons was between 14 and 18. However, the older people from the centre used to come early for coffee. They were older people and it was expresso Italian coffee and it was very high quality, and I would sit with them and then they would go on their business and I on my own. But, otherwise, when the dusk fell, I had the youth. Sometimes I was the oldest person who would walk in there, and sometimes I would not stay there very much. I had younger waiters, young men and women. It was for the youth. There were no folk music there which was what people mostly listened to in Bosnia. I was getting music cassettes from abroad, from my brother or somebody else, so it was mostly disco or music from abroad. This is what they were interested in, the youth there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is right that your ethnic background is described as being Serbian, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As a Serb opening a coffee bar in Kozarac at this time, did you employ people of different ethnic backgrounds to work there with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. The whole time while the business was open, I never had more than two waiters. However, one was always a Muslim, the entire time. The other one could have been any other nationality, but one waiter would always be a Muslim. I did that on advice, for the most part, of my neighbours who were natives there. It was reasoning that I would not want to create an impression that this was a Serb cafe. It was for all the people of Kozarac, and mostly Muslims went there, if that is what you are asking about their national background. As far as I could notice, I never polemicized about that and I never kept any statistics who was coming. But, since I was born in Kozarac, I lived there, 98 per cent of people there were Muslim. Many Serbs, I do not know why, but they were not coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Given the costs that were involved in building these premises and running them, could your business have been successful if it had only restricted those who were welcome there to being those only of Serbian background?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no, not even -- I can count how many Serbs came, maybe seven or eight. Sometimes it was a cafe -- there were always 100 or sometimes over 200 people there every night, I cannot tell, because I did the finances, I know what the turnover was there, how much beverages had been used. So I know that my average was between 100 and 200, and in Kozarac you did not have enough Serbs in that period. Especially in 1991, a lot of Serbs and young men who were potential patrons were in different war zones around Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: With the cafe running, were you able to repay the loans that you had obtained from some of the local people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know if you understood me well. Every once in a while I would get money, but I would also loan money to others. Of course, I would always return money. There were no -- it was my business was always clean that way, but it would happen that one of either Sefik Arnautovic or Adil Jakupovic -- in Yugoslavia, you always had a problem with foreign currency, and the dinar would lose about 30 per cent of the value at a time. Often, people would come and ask one, two or 3,000 deutschemarks at a time. That would be my daily intake and they needed it for a man who was exchanging 20 or 30,000 marks for them, and then they would give me the counter value in dinars the next day.
