So this is how we exchanged, so there was no problem there. But whether I could keep in business if my patrons were only Serbs, that is a silly question; you could not even think about that. It is well-known the structure of the population in Kozarac, plus I never thought of who would be my patrons in my cafe.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Just to clear up one matter, although the dinar was the official currency in the former Yugoslavia, would it be right to say that a lot of business was really done with deutschemarks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, mostly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The other section of the house that your brother Ljubomir had given to him, did that open as business premises as well?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Precisely, because Ljubo saw that my business is taking off and it was successful, I suggested to him that he should do something similar and I suggested I know that he was -- that my neighbour, Adil Jakupovic, was in a dilemma. He said, "How is that possible?" He did not want to take that risk to open up a private business. I know that he often told me later that because of my advice he took that road and that was after me. So, also Ljubo, because of my suggestions, opened a private business in that former residential part of our old family house. He opened it, I think it was somewhere 15, 20 days before the war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What business did he open there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His business was linked to the brewery in Banja Luka. He made a business arrangement. They would ship the goods to him on a regular basis. He would distribute it. He would have a certain percentage from distribution. So that was wholesale, so he was distributing wholesale. So it was not a bottle or two or three but larger quantities and through that, and that was the practice in the Prijedor municipality. From such distribution centres others would supply. For instance, if I wanted some beverages, I would buy with him, of course, or somebody else because it was much cheaper. It was like a factory price. It was as if you bought it in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He described it as a beer discount store. Would that be a correct description?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I think that that was the official title. He should know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he also sell soft drinks there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was his business in that 21 days or so before the war started in Kozarac successful in that short period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did it look as though that was a business, if allowed to continue, would have been something that would have continued to have been successful in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is certain. I had some acquaintances in Prijedor who in a short period of time became rich doing this kind of business. I think it was an excellent business. I think it was better than the one I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that looks to be an appropriate moment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We will stand in recess for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Thank you, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions now about your relationships with the other residents of Kozarac. Were you on friendly terms with most people there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you a person who mixed with people from Croatian backgrounds, Muslims ----

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Excuse me one moment, Mr. Kay. I am just checking to see if there is sound going to the gallery. Yes, it is coming through now. I am sorry, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is all right, your Honour. I will just start the last question again. [To the witness]: Were you someone who mixed with people who were Croats or Muslims or other ethnic backgrounds within Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I did not make any differences in terms of ethnic origin. That was how our father brought us up, both me and my other brothers. I paid no attention. I may have had friends of Serb nationality, but most of my friends were Muslims and Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Living within Kozarac, would it have been difficult for you to restrict yourself to friendships with only Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, it is hard to answer that question, because there were few Serbs of my generation. I do not think anyone -- in my childhood, in elementary school, they were all Muslims. I did not have a Serb friend.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In the ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember a single Serb with whom I was close, that we used to visit each other at home. No, I cannot remember a single one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did that present you with any particular problems, any particular difficulty, in life or was it something that was just natural and you were able to deal with?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I simply did not pay attention to such things. The people I was friendly with also, we never talked about such things. We never had any polemics. That was how I was brought up, as I said, me and my brothers. I also, when we are talking about this, let me add I was not christened. We are not religious people. We did not celebrate religious feasts. We celebrated the state holidays of the former Yugoslavia which were the same for all ethnic groups. There was no difference. I do not know how he declared himself officially, but I do not remember myself or any of my friends ever discussing ethnic differences. This was something we simply did not pay any attention to.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did your cafe bar in the months just before the conflict in Kozarac become a place that was a focus, a centre, for those who were of Serbian background who had returned from the front, who had been fighting in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not think it was ever a centre for one particular ethnic group, particularly not the military. The military would go to cafes where good quality food was being served, not just drinks. In those days the soldiers were well paid in '91. As I said earlier, my cafe was a place where the young people would come. I cannot say that occasionally older people did not come by, they did, but only rarely. They spent a short time there. They did not enjoy disco music. They were not interested in pop songs. They were interested in the songs glorifying nationalist leaders, and my cafe was never a meeting place for such guests. Sometimes people from the Territorial Defence would drop in, members of the JNA perhaps, but this was not a gathering place that was happening in other restaurants or cafes where food was being served, Neira, Red Roses. The guests were mostly people who had plenty of money, who were ready to spend it on food. My guests were young men and women who had pocket money given by their parents to spend that evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You mentioned Neira and Red Roses, were they other cafes in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These two that I mentioned, they are not cafes, they are restaurants, and I mentioned them because that was where food was served. In cafes, food was not served, as a rule. There were other cafes, but the army, the military, would mainly go to these two restaurants. I never heard that there were any problems there either. I went there rarely, but whenever I did, it was packed to capacity with guests with various insignia of all kinds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We have heard of a friendship you had with a man called Emir Karabasic. When did you first meet him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I met Emir Karabasic in 1980 or '81, when I became leader of the karate club in Kozarac. I first met his younger brother, Esmir, and then Emir. I do not know, but later we found out that my father and his grandfather had somehow close relations. They were both participants in the Second World War and had very good and close relations, and those relationships between the elders were always passed on to the younger generations. Emir Karabasic graduated secondary school in Sarajevo. He returned to the Prijedor municipality. He worked at a time in Prijedor. Then he worked in Omarska for four or five times, then for a time in Ljubija. That is it, as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The work you described, was that Emir Karabasic working as a police officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We saw a photograph when your wife gave evidence. Perhaps D71 could be put on the overhead projector, so that it is made clear? Perhaps Miss Sutherland may be able to assist? I know she can work the machine. Thank you. We see there a photograph of the family on holiday apparently taken by you, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: That is your wife and your eldest daughter Valentina with your eldest brother Stojan, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Emir is sitting on the towels behind your wife, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So, your friendship with him was a friendship where you went on holiday together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our friendship was much greater than many are aware of. Relations between me and this older brother, for instance, were blood relationships, but with Karabasic and some of my great friends, we would visit each other, spend the night, eat at each other's houses, his problems were mine and my problems were his. They were our common problems. He was like a brother to me, and I think he considered me the same. This was a photograph when we went to the seaside together. It was taken in Medulin, near Pula, in Croatia. I think we spent about three weeks together at the seaside. I do not know what else I could say, but we slept in the same room. We shared the same room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: What would the date of that holiday have been?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think this was taken in 1983. We went to the seaside together several times. This was not the first time. We would go to Belgrade, to various places. It is difficult to remember each of those trips, but any family festivity or reunion at my home could not take place without him and his wife attending. They knew -- he knew all my friends in Banja Luka, in Prijedor. He was like a member of the family. Paolo and Vesna, when they would come to Banja Luka, would say, "Invite Karabasic" and I would go and call him because we could not have any get together without him. We were together in sports too, but it was not at the level that people may think. His brother was a much better karatist, but he and I were friends. We were much closer otherwise, not in sports. On a Saturday morning, he would come at 5 o'clock and we would run towards Mount Kozara jogging, then we would come back and we had some wonderful times together.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your wife said that he was a single man who had many girlfriends. Did he have a wife? Was he married or did he have a steady girlfriend?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is hard to say. As in my case I got married, but not officially. The moment we made our vows to each other, we considered ourselves married. We did not consider a paper to be important. Anyway, in Yugoslavia any extra marital community had equal status as an official marriage. Emir Karabasic was in a similar situation. He did have a wife, but in 1990 he lost a baby upon delivery. I was in Banja Luka then. I was staying with my friends, Selcek(?). We had a road accident so we went back to Banja Luka. This was a terrible blow for him and for me, of course. After that, the relationship between him and his wife at the time cooled, so that afterwards one could say he was married or he was not. The death of the baby contributed to the collapse of that union. That is why probably my wife thought that he was sometimes married, sometimes not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When your father Ostoja died, was he one of the bearers of the coffin at your father's funeral?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Who were the other bearers of your father's coffin?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly friends, my brothers, among others, Vercek Paolo, my friend from Banja Luka. I will never forget it. We bathed my father when he died. Karabasic carried him out. They were -- we were always at each other's side when we were in difficulty and when we were enjoying ourselves. Karabasic was there all the time, not just he, but many other of my friends and neighbours. My friends from elementary school, they came to attend the funeral from various parts of Yugoslavia, not just those living there at the time. In our parts, funerals, weddings, are a time to show respect towards one's neighbours and it is something one remembers, one never forgets.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before the conflict in Kozarac on 24th May 1992, how would you describe your friendship with Emir Karabasic at that stage, at that point of time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the beginning -- at the end of 1991, at the beginning of 1992, Emir Karabasic had many personal problems. In the middle of 1989 he was working as a policeman in Omarska for four years by then and I was familiar with all of his problems. At that time, he led a karate group in Lamovita and Omarska. He spent many years living and working there, and I do not know the reasons, but for six months Karabasic was suspended as a policeman at the end of '91/beginning of '92, and he immediately appealed to me and my brother to try and help him to move to Banja Luka or to some other town. I do not know the real reasons why he was suspended as a policeman, but I know that he was laid off for six months. He fought for that job because he always said that was the only thing he knew how to do. My relationship towards him did not change, but he was very busy with his own personal problems. I do not know whether they had to do with Omarska or Kozarac. Many of his colleagues did not like him. They reported against him. They claimed that he acted contrary to the policemen's code. He was an honest policeman on duty, and when he was off duty he was like anybody else who liked company. Probably some of his colleagues did not like this and they complained against him. It happened in Omarska and in Kozarac too. They would go to higher level authorities to report him. Our relationships at the time did not change particularly, but we did not see each other so often because of those personal problems. I remember that he came on several occasions to see me and my wife. Whenever he passed by, he would drop in. He would often bring cevapcici, minced meatballs. Maybe he had problems because he was a great friend of mine, I do not know really, but in any case we did not see each other very often then. I attributed this to the problems that he was having in the police because he often told me about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: He was of Muslim ethnic background, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was a Muslim but he considered himself a Yugoslav, a typical Yugoslav.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: As a policeman working in Omarska, that would have been him working within a particular village that had a concentration of Serbian people and Serbian policemen within the town, would that be right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Karabasic worked in Ormaska for four or five years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Omarska, unlike Kozarac, was a particular area that had a concentration of Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was similar to Kozarac in the sense that in Kozarac there was a larger percentage of Muslims and in Omarska there was a much larger percentage of Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said that your relationship changed between the two of you, but was there any animosity, was there any dislike, or was it that he had problems at that particular time and your friendship for that period was not based upon the same previous friendship that you had had before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I still think that even at the time that he was my best friend and I his. Our relationships did not change particularly. As I said, maybe the atmosphere in those parts had changed and it required everyone to take care of himself. I did not have much time to roam around. I did not dare to as I did before; I spent most of my time at home or in my cafe or visiting family in Banja Luka, and Karabasic too was working in Ljubija at that time. This is another part of the municipality of Prijedor. But our relationships did not change. We would always meet, talk about all kinds of things. We just did not see each other so often because out of technical reasons this was no longer possible. Karabasic worked in Omarska. We would see each other through sport, and then he moved to Ljubija. Sports activities died down. Ljubija was quite far away, but our relationship did not change. I know when his brother died in a traffic accident I attended the funeral. We talked. I know I was upset. This was just a few months before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did he ever serve in Kozarac before the war -- now I am just talking about in 1992 -- as a policeman in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not think so. We never talked about it, about the police too much, and I am not sure, to be perfectly honest. Our conversation was usually about private problems, sports or family relations, what happened within my family and my friends and his friends. That was our -- that was our conversation. We never had special conversations about my business and he about his own. All our conversations were unofficial in character. It was private in nature, like with a family member, we never polemicized much about anything, but I do not think he worked in Kozarac, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: You said in answer to an earlier question that the atmosphere had changed in the area. Can you, as far as you are concerned, give a time when it was detectable that the atmosphere in Kozarac had changed from what it had been in the old days?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the atmosphere in Kozarac was no different from the one that was around in all of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I do not know exactly when this Assembly was constituted, the multi-party one, but I remember that those proceedings were televised, that people were talking among themselves. They had fears. The conflicts in Sarajevo somehow, they were spreading to other parts. The conflicts that were there, they were frightening people, if you look from that propaganda angle. On the other hand, the war in Croatia was a fact, and from day-to-day you could see that it was moving towards Bosnia. It was a fact with which we lived. We were all fearing that it would spill over into Bosnia, and the President there said that they would do anything to move the war into Bosnia and, in essence, this is what actually happened. People lived in fear. There was a general fear.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did there come a time when you, in fact, received a threatening letter whilst you were in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that happened in August of 1990, around the time of the death of my father.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It has been suggested by some witnesses that were called at an earlier stage in the proceedings that either you or your wife had written this letter as some sort of gesture, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Not at all, neither myself nor my wife wrote this, nor do I know who wrote this. I do not know who wrote this letter. I received that letter. It is a fact, it happened. It can happen to anybody. I never hid that -- for the first few days I did hide. I did not want anybody to know in the family. Then I thought about it and I felt, somehow my conscience woke up and if something did happen I would have felt guilty that I did not say about that, and those threats were also directed not only at me but my mother, my wife and I lived in Kozarac at the time with my mother and my wife and two children, and I was afraid for their security. At that time when it was not right for me to hide, then I showed it to my wife and my mother and I called my brothers to ask them what to do and I wanted to leave. However, I talked to my neighbours who were Muslims and members of SDA Party, and they said, not to pay any attention to that, that they would support me, that there was no problem. I asked the veterans' union representative and I invited him to my house and we talked, and I talked to Mr. Kahrimanovic with Adil Jakupovic. I talked to a lot of my neighbours and I wanted to find a real solution because it would not have been fair of me to have left a place as if I was expelled. I did not want that. The only thing I could do was I turned the letter over to the police in Prijedor, and I did not want something to happen and I did not -- I had not done something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In August 1990 when you received that letter, had you had any indications before that date that certain people might be viewing you with animosity or dislike?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will tell you. After my father's death and especially after I decided to build the business premises in Kozarac when it was visible that I would open this cafe, because before I was thinking I wanted to go abroad, that was my long time wish, but I never succeeded for a number of years. Then I decided to continue my life in Kozarac and then I decided to invest everything I had into that. I do not know. Since I started building this cafe, some things started. There were some things that were happening that reminded me that there were some people there who did not want me to continue my life there. To date, I do not know who it was. I think it could have been the competition of other cafe owners. I do not think it was a movement or anything. I thought it about it for a long time. Maybe somebody interpreted it that way. I think that that was a bit false, this letter. I did not -- I thought it was a provocation. It could have been done by anybody. After all, it could have been done by Serbs. It was all possible. I did not -- I could not find out a solution about it. As far as the relationships are concerned later on, sometimes there were phone threats to my daughter or my wife. Once I picked up that phone and I talked to this person who had called, and it seemed silly to me, but my daughter was afraid and so my wife. I did not pay much attention to it, but especially through the accent, I could figure out it was nobody from that area. I thought it was somebody from abroad. It was not an accent of a person who lives in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was a female and it was ridiculous, what the voice was saying, and it effected my family much more than it did me. I did not speak about it much to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At this time from 1990 was there suddenly more political activity within Kozarac and the area of Prijedor generally? Were people identifying themselves for the first time with political parties in a way that they had never experienced before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would not say that was the case. I think from the very beginning of the creation of the national parties, for instance, SDA, SDS, HDZ, those parties were representing themselves in public as if they were to co-operate in the future, that the main enemy was the former communist system, that that was their priority. All parties proclaimed that, both the nationalist ones and the others, and they were leaving an impression among common people that the important thing was to defeat communism and their relationships would be splendid; as if in the former system the nations did not have their representatives and now they would represent them, especially HDZ and SDS and SDA. That is how people also thought. So it was generally a movement. In the beginning it did not seem to me like a party organisation. There were movements, one can say, and the Croats mostly joined HDZ and the Serbs SDS and Muslims to the SDA. That is how it started. The relations among people and this taking memberships in these parties did not cause discord among common people. I do not know a single case when people came into a conflict because one was a member of HDZ or SDS or SDA. There were no such cases. I do not know any of these parties had platforms that would hurt -- be hurtful to other nations. I do not know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When did you join the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was that before or after you had received that letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was later. Not only after I received the letter, but several months later it turned out that the investigation that allegedly was conducted was fruitless. Then there were several additional phone calls and threats, and my wife insisted that we had to take some shelter with some side. Then we went to Prijedor to the health centre and that Dragoje Musac(?) was working there. He said that they would take us in and so we became members, my wife, myself and my brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The Prosecution in this case have quoted from a document that you wrote saying that you were one of the first members of the SDS in the Prijedor region. Do you know if that is right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Theoretically, that was impossible. Up until the establishment of the local committee of the party, I was not a member of any SDS or HDZ or SDA. You have to be a member of this local committee, go to meetings and be part of the committee. Membership of a party is nothing. It would be almost like an honorary membership. I was not a member of any local committee. There was no local committee, and I could not have attended meetings in Prijedor in any local committee. That was the procedure. So there was no dilemma there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: In November 1991, there was a plebiscite held for Serbian people. Is it right that you conducted that plebiscite on behalf of the SDS in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that that is not the right definition.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Perhaps then you can ----

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That reflects the real situation. The fact of the matter is that probably the SDS was the initiator of the plebiscite. . I think that the initiative for the plebescite came from the SDS. However, all this was conducted through the Local Assembly in Prijedor. There was a Commission of the Municipal Assembly that was in charge to organise the plebescite. I do not know what the procedure was to be followed at the municipal level, the party and the Municipal Assembly, but the party itself could not have organised such a plebiscite. The party could table it, but there is a commission for plebiscite. Non-partisan members had to be appointed and I think that the control of this plebiscite, one of the people who controlled it was Jovan Vukoje and this man was not a member of the SDS. I think he was a socialist or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: If we could have a look at Exhibit 146 and at the same time if you could pull out 147. If 146 could be put on the monitor. If you could put the English version on the monitor and give the defendant the copy in his own language. Thank you very much. I hope that can be read by everyone. This document here is the decision on the appointment of voting officials for the plebiscite in the area of Kozarac, Vidovici, and you were to be the President of the voting officials. The document is actually dated 8th November 1991 and signed by Dragan Savanovic. Can you tell us how it was that you came about to be appointed with this position and this responsibility? Whose decision was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to say that at the top of the document here it is clearly stated that the organiser of this was commissioned, a municipal plebiscite commission, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Is that a municipal plebescite commission of Prijedor or elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Exactly as I said. It is the municipal commission that was appointed by the Municipal Assembly. I do not know the procedure, but I assume that the suggestion came from the SDS within the Assembly, and then based on that suggestion this commission was established who took over the responsibility for this plebiscite, the same way for the referendum that the SDA initiated. They could not do themselves, so it was all down at the municipal level. Again, a commission was formed that was put in charge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you approached by someone beforehand and asked if you would undertake this responsibility, or were you just notified in some way that you would be expected to undertake this responsibility?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I remember exactly how it took place. At that time in Kozarac, as in other places in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there were some multi-party governments. There were a few representatives of different parties in this Executive Committee. The SDS was represented by Zivko Kos from the village of Balte, Babici or Balte, I do not know exactly. At that time both Balte and Babici were belonging to the Local Commune of Kozarac. As far as I know, they already had previously formed SDS committees there. Based on that Zivko Kos who was a member of the Council of Local Commune of Kozarac, at that time he visited me and asked me whether I would undertake with some people to organise this plebiscite at voting station 36 which was in Vidovici. Here it states clearly that this is voting station 36. In the Local Commune in Kozarac there were at least five or six such polling stations, so this would be one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: This document refers to polling place No. 36 in Vidovici. Were there other such documents such as this that indicated other polling places for this plebiscite?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Here is mentioned Kozarac, Vidovici, as you can see, but mostly it was planned that the plebiscite would be held in the village of Vidovici which has seven families living there. Because of that it was not practical for them to go to Kamicani, to another place, so that is why it had been suggested that this polling station be formed there. It was assumed that there were only a few families of Serb background that lived there. So it was expected that there would not be many votes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So was your responsibility as the President of the voting officials for the plebiscite also concerned with the other polling stations around Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. This was only for the polling station 36, but not for Kozarac. It is only for the village of Vidovici. However, we organised that in an office that was in the churchyard in Kozarac. The only reason for that was because there were no other communal objects, and it would not have been right to hold the plebiscite in a private house. So we went to this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: So would it be right to say that Vidovici in fact did not have a polling place No. 36 on plebiscite day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct. Another reason for holding this in the centre of Kozarac, it seemed to me that to organise a plebiscite in a Serb village would not be right in Kozarac, since I lived in the centre of Kozarac. It seemed to me to be like some kind of clandestine voting. It would not have been fair. That was one of the reasons why we decided that the plebiscite take place in Kozarac. It would be questionable to hold the voting in a single ethnic group, place. I did not think it was right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Can we look now at Exhibit 147. Could the Serbo-Croatian version be put in front of the defendant and the English version on the monitor. This is headed as the Minutes of the Election Committee for the day of the plebiscite on 9th November. I think you have already told us that this took place actually in the Serbian Orthodox church office in Kozarac, that is right, is it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in the church, but an office in the churchyard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I meant. If the English version can now be pushed further up the monitor, please, so we have the bottom half of the page fully on display. Thank you very much. This is a record of the numbers of people who voted. Was this a particular responsibility of checking the ballot for the day by you and your committee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not just me that had to do that. I was President of the commission who had to supervise to make sure that everything was in order, but since it lasted two days many people took turns, not just those on the list; there were many others who took turns. After the voting we acted according to the procedure. There was a document indicating the actual procedure for packing and counting the ballots. They had to be packed and then after a certain time sent to the Municipal Assembly in Prijedor. They were not sent to party headquarters, but to the Municipal Assembly and its commission responsible for organising the plebiscite in the municipality of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At this time in November 1991 were you someone who had read a great deal of the political text, other documents that were issued by the party of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I never read anything linked to the SDS or to any other party. In the first place, I had no access to the documents of the SDS party. I was not a member of any local committee, as I said, so I do not see how I could have participated in any such activities. I am not aware of any publications made nor did I ever receive any such documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Was the scale of the SDS in Kozarac a very small scale operation without a great deal of organisation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was no SDS in Kozarac until 1992. This is quite clear. Furthermore, many people who were members of the SDS did not proclaim their affiliation in public. I personally did not know who was a member, nor did many know that I was a member. I paid membership fees once and never again. Then I lost my little booklet, membership booklet. So my membership in the SDS in that period was quite insignificant. They must have kept a record in Prijedor of members and I was on that record, on that register, but there was no SDS active in Kozarac at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: We know that in August 1992 you eventually became the President of the SDS in Kozarac. I am not now concerned with that period, but the period before the conflict. Did you have any official position within the party before the conflict started in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I told you that until the conflict started in 1992 there was no local SDS committee in Kozarac, officially or unofficially. As far as I am aware, the closest local committee of the SDS was in Jaruge or Babici or somewhere there, but in the centre of Kozarac where I lived there was no SDS local committee registered, nor were any meetings of the SDS party held. Officially the local committee of the SDS was registered in December 1992. That is quite evident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: At this time before the conflict in May 1992, did you attend any political assemblies in Prijedor which would have involved the SDS? Did you attend any of their meetings?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, could you please repeat the period you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before the conflict in Kozarac did you attend any of the meetings of the SDS in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never attended any meeting of the SDS. It could not have happened. I do not know how to explain it to you. If you were not a member of a local committee you could not attend such a meeting. I know this because the procedure for attending meetings was the same procedure as existed during the communist system. There were local organisations of the League of Communists and these local organisations had a list of members. People were called you out and it was their duty to attend those meetings. Several absences without justification would entail dismissal from the party. Another obligation was to pay membership fees. That was one of the most important duties. If you were irregular in your payment of fees you would be deleted from the register. I am saying this because I think that a similar procedure existed in all other parties. I was not a member of any local committee, and if I wanted to I could not attend such meetings. Every member could attend assembly meetings of the Serbian Democratic Party that were held once a year, but I did not attend ever such assemblies either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did you have high contacts within the SDS party, with people who were officials?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that the highest official I knew was called Zivko Kos, that is as much as I knew, but I did not have special contacts with other people. Of course, I learnt from the media who was President of the party, the SDS party, but I did not have any special relationships with any of them. I know from the time the parties were formed that the relations among the party leaders were good. Then later I do not know what happened with those relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did they supply you as an individual with any information as to what they were doing, what they were planning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, I did not even have a statute. I assume there must have existed a statute of the party. I do not know. I am not aware of it. However, no one ever showed it to me or read from it to me. I do not know what the programme of those political parties were, any of the parties. I was not really interested to be quite frank.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When the takeover of Prijedor took place on 29th April 1992 and the organs of power within Prijedor were subject to the control of the SDS, were you aware of that event before it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I heard of it for the first time I think it was a Thursday. I remember hearing about it from my neighbours. The first to tell me was Adil Jakupovic. A large number of people from Kozarac were turned back from their way to work. They were turned back to Kozarac. They simply could not go to work on that day and that is when I heard from them for the first time that there had been a takeover of power, that relations had become strained. I do not know the reason, but I know for sure that many were turned back. They told me that they had been turned back from entering Prijedor. I saw lots of people going by and I enquired and many neighbours told me this. I never listened to the radio, but I heard about it from the neighbours that I saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Were you in Prijedor on that day of 29th April? Did you take any part in taking over the institutions of the town either on that day or on the days afterwards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Did anyone invite you to take part in the takeover of the institutions within Prijedor on that day or the days immediately following?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I do not see why. What could I have done? What could I have helped? In what way could I have helped? I do not think the idea had ever struck anyone. There was no point, no reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: When that takeover occurred, what effect did it have on the people within a town such as Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People did feel upset. I spoke to many neighbours then. I think it was done in an unfair manner. People were surprised, more perhaps because those political parties ever since their foundation had managed to convince the average citizen that they were co-operating, that there was not any chance of anything happening. They kept advocating the idea that what was most important was to overcome the communist system. There was a general euphoria and you could frequently see people sitting together belonging to different parties, drinking and saying, "We have defeated communism". Ordinary people were not aware of where it was all leading.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Before that takeover took place on 29th April, had your family left Kozarac for any substantial period of time to live elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on April 1st.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why was that on April 1st?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several months before that, maybe ever since March, people were getting armed. After the last few months people would not even hide their weapons. They would walk in the streets armed and there was general chaos. The more serious people would not carry weapons in public, but the younger generations would not conceal their weapons. They were getting organised in a sense. I know there were many lists of who would go to which shelter. They were listing buildings. Nobody informed me about anything, I was never invited. I simply felt isolated in that period. Furthermore, I noticed that anyone who had anywhere to go had left, particularly those who had a member of the family abroad, Germany or Slovenia. People were leaving en masse and it was very difficult to get a bus ticket at the time. Those from Banja Luka going to Belgrade were full too. Whoever had anywhere to go went. I simply had no other place to go to. So I sent my family. My wife arranged with a friend of hers that they go to Sanski Most. People were on the move. People were leaving.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Why were weapons and arms suddenly being visible and able to be seen in Kozarac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the real answer to that question. Perhaps if I look back at all that happened, I think that everything that was happening in Sarajevo created fear in people. The war in Croatia was getting closer. People felt scared. They feared one another. Then there were groups that emerged, people with a criminal past, for example, Suljo Kusuran who had served time in prison for many years on the Serb side. There were some extremists in Prijedor too and these groups created this fear among people. They would fire shots. They would act in an unruly manner. I knew that people would sell a car to buy a rifle. They would build dug-outs next to their homes. That I could understand because people remembered the last war and the weapons were probably because they feared for their family, but to carry weapons, that was most unpleasant to see, particularly in an environment in which there were five or six families that were Serb in my street, the street I was living in. I think my house was the only Serb house. So that was one of the reasons why I sent my family to Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Your Honour, that is a convenient moment.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Wladimiroff, I have been told that you wish that the Trial Chamber meet on Monday?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: That is right, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: We are at your disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: It might be better. You will need that time to complete your witnesses, will you not? Do you think you will finish by Tuesday?

utterances.speaker: MR. WLADIMIROFF
utterances.text: We will aim to do that, but it would be very helpful if we can sit on Monday indeed.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Mr. Niemann, I will ask if there is any objection. Is there any?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIEMANN
utterances.text: No, your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE PRESIDING JUDGE
utterances.text: Very good, then we will. We did discuss the closing arguments. The Trial Chamber has decided that the only date I suppose that will fit with both of the schedules of the Prosecutor and the Defence, since you are not available on 14th (and then the courtroom is being used by the other Chamber on 19th and 20th) would be November 25th. So we want the closing arguments to begin on Monday, November 25th at 10 a.m. If you wish to submit written submissions then those should be filed by November 20th. As we have indicated, it would be very helpful to us in either the written submissions or orally that you give references and charts or outlines, however you want to do it. In the written submission, of course, you will need to discuss the facts and how they relate to the law, the elements. Do not forget about Article 7(1). That was not mentioned in either of the pretrial briefs. Do not forget about the nature of the conflict, internationality. Perhaps we can talk more about it, but I wanted to give those dates, November 25th at 10 a.m. for the closing arguments. Written submissions are to be filed on 20th. We will adjourn until Monday at 10 a.m. (5.30 p.m.).
